paragraphs.text: Commentary § 10.52:1 Rule 10.52 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.52. In Schitthelm v. Kelemen, 2013 ABQB 42, 2013 CarswellAlta 239, 557 A.R. 151, 278 C.R.R. (2d) 235, Justice Yamauchi provided a comprehensive summary of the law regarding contempt. His Lordship said: B. — The Nature of the Contempt Power 19 Superior courts have the inherent jurisdiction to control the proceedings before them. For a court to operate effectively, it requires an ability to maintain order in its proceedings and ensure its directions are followed. This is part of the rule of law. 20 Courts have differentiated between contempt of a civil nature and contempt of a criminal nature: see e.g. Poje v. British Columbia (Attorney General), [1953] 1 SCR 516 at 517 [Poje]; United Nurses of Alberta v. Alberta (Attorney General), [1992] 1 SCR 901 at 931 [United Nurses]; Chiang (Trustee of) v. Chiang, 2009 ONCA 3 at para 10, 93 OR (3d) 483 and Seaward v. Paterson, [1897] 1 Ch 545 at 555-56, 559. However, in Vidéotron Ltée v. Industries Microlec Products Électioniques Inc, [1992] 2 SCR 1065 at 1075 [Vidéotron], Gonthier J warns that “too great an insistence on the distinction between civil contempt and criminal contempt” could mask characteristics common to all types of contempt. In Pro Swing Inc v. Elta Golf Inc, 2006 SCC 52 at para 34, [2006] 2 SCR 612 [Pro Swing], the Supreme Court of Canada states that the decision in Vidéotron set “aside the distinction between the civil and criminal aspects” of contempt law. Why is this? As mentioned in R. v. Cohn (1984), 48 OR (2d) 65 at para 11 [Cohn]: … the [Criminal] Code does not specifically provide for or define any such offence nor does it set forth any procedure for the prosecution of such offence or any penalty following conviction therefor. Resort must be had to the common law for these matters. Contempt of court is a common law offence. Thus, contempt, whether of a criminal or civil nature derives from the same source, the common law. Certainly, the context in which each occurs might differ, and the results that flow from each might inform whether the contempt is “civil” or “criminal.” However, as noted in Halsbury's Laws of England, vol 22, 5th ed (London, UK: LexisNexis, 2012) at para 2, footnote 1 [citations omitted], “[t]he classification of contempts as criminal or civil has become progressively less important and has been described as ‘unhelpful and almost meaningless’ in the present day”. 21 Vidéotron and Pro Swing indicate that contempt should not be looked at as merely “civil or “criminal” in nature, because all contempt has a public aspect and is of a “quasi-criminal nature”: Pro Swing at para 36. 22 While courts have held that civil contempt is generally coercive in nature and criminal contempt punitive in nature, this Court is not convinced that the procedural rights that attach to contempt proceedings and the Charter's applicability to them change merely because of the way in which one classifies the contempt. In all cases, courts must examine the particular facts before them and determine the procedures that natural justice and the Charter require. C. — Charter Applicability 23 The Charter is engaged when a person's liberty is at risk: see e.g. Re BC Motor Vehicle Act, [1985] 2 SCR 486. In a contempt application, a person's liberty may be at risk: Rules rr 10.53(1)(a)–(c). Is the Charter engaged when a person faces a finding that they are in civil contempt pursuant to the Rules? … 25 Has a person who is alleged to have committed civil contempt been “charged” with anything? In Cohn at 75–76, the Ontario Court of Appeal said: The heading which precedes s. 11 of the Charter reads: “Proceedings in criminal and penal matters”. The portion of s. 11 which determines in the first instance the persons who may derive the benefit thereof is the first line which states: “Any person charged with an offence has the right …”. The heading to s. 11 makes it clear that s. 11 of the Charter applies to an offence although it may not be, strictly speaking, a criminal matter. It is sufficient if it is a penal matter. Even if contempt proceedings are not properly characterized as criminal matters, there can be no doubt that they must, at the very least, be characterized as penal matters. The word “penal” as used in the heading undoubtedly bears the dictionary meaning “of, pertaining to or relating to punishment”. It is the power to punish for contempt of court which is expressly preserved by s. 8 of the Criminal Code and, as previously stated, I am of the view that the citation for contempt of court constitutes the charging of an offence within the meaning of s. 11. It follows, therefore, that s. 11(c) and (d) of the Charter are applicable to contempt of court proceedings. 26 While one might think that, in a civil matter, the party making the application to have the court find the other party in civil contempt simply wants to have the court order enforced for its benefit, there can be no doubt that Rules rr 10.53(1)(b) and 10.53(1)(c) are penal in nature. The spectre of that punishment alone makes the Rules that govern civil contempt subject to the Charter, or at least some of its provisions. See e.g. R. v. Winter (1986), 72 AR 164 at para 9 [Winter], where the Alberta Court of Appeal chose not to follow a decision of the Québec Superior Court in Attorney-General of Quebec v. Laurendeau (1982), 3 CCC (3d) 250, which held that a person cited for contempt was not “charged” with an offence within the meaning of Charter s 11. In Placentia-St. Mary's Roman Catholic School Board v. Newfoundland Association of Public Employees, Local 5802 (1986), 60 Nfld & PEIR 350 at para 4 (Nfld SC (TD)), Steele J said “[t]he penalty for contempt of court may involve a fine or committal to jail and is therefore a punishment affecting the liberty of the person. Consequently contempt proceedings may have definite overtones of a criminal nature.” At paragraph 5, Steele J went on to quote, with agreement, the following passage from Nigel Lowe & Sir Gordon Borrie, Borrie & Lowe's Law of Contempt, 2nd ed (London, UK: Butterworths, 1983) at 393, where the authors said: Although this aspect of contempt is designated civil, because of the penal sanctions, it has been said to “partake of a criminal nature” and many of the rules that normally apply when seeking to prove an accused guilty of a crime, apply when seeking to show that the defendant has committed civil contempt. It also means that the rules safeguarding contemners'[sic] rights must be strictly complied with. [Footnotes omitted.] 27 Even if one concedes that Charter rights are engaged, does this provide a complete answer to the question concerning the procedures a court must use in contempt proceedings? The Charter itself comes with built-in limits. Charter s 7 provides that every right contained in that section is subject to restrictions that are in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice. As well, every Charter right can be limited by engaging Charter s 1, which provides for “such reasonable limits prescribed by law as can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society.” Indeed, in Winter at para 12, the Alberta Court of Appeal found the instanter procedure which the trial judge used to find the accused in contempt was justified under Charter s. 1. 28 In a civil contempt proceeding, the court may not discard the alleged contemnor's rights. The court must, however, carefully balance those rights against those of the party who alleges that the alleged contemnor has committed civil contempt. Above all, when a court considers the procedural requirements that are engaged in a civil contempt proceeding, it must ensure that the alleged contemnor is not found to have committed contempt without adequate proof of culpability. This informs all aspects of contempt procedure. 29 The procedure required to address the competing interests in contempt applications will not always remain constant; each case depends on its particular facts. D. — Procedure 30 In R. v. K(B), [1995] 4 SCR 186 at para 11 [K(B)], Lamer CJ said: In order to simplify matters, it is my opinion that we should use the notion of citing in contempt, not as an expression of a finding of contempt but instead, as a method of providing the accused with notice that he or she has been contemptuous and will be required to show cause why they should not be held in contempt. 31 While the cases that deal with criminal contempt are distinguishable from civil contempt under the Rules, they are instructive in assisting the courts in fashioning a procedure to use when considering an allegation of civil contempt. What emerges from those cases, and what natural justice and the Charter require, is a three-stage procedure: citing the person in contempt of the court, conviction and sentencing. Under the Rules, those stages are specifically outlined as follows: Citing the person in contempt of the court: Rules rr 10.52(1) and 10.52(2) require the accuser provide the alleged contemnor with notice of the application for a declaration of civil contempt; Conviction: Rules r 10.52(3) allows the judge to “declare” the alleged contemnor to be in civil contempt; Sentencing: Rules r 10.53 outlines the “penalties” and “sanctions” the judge might impose on the contemnor. 32 Each stage should be separated, unless there is an urgent and imperative reason why the stages should be collapsed so the procedure can be expedited: R. v. Arradi, 2003 SCC 23 at para 30, [2003] 1 SCR 280 [Arradi]; Doobay v. Diamond, 2012 ONCA 580 at para 40, leave to appeal to SCC requested. As well, the Rules provide that a judge may cite and declare the person to be in contempt instanter in appropriate circumstances: Winter. … 33 Except in the case of a judge using an instanter summary procedure, this procedure allows, among other things, the alleged contemnor to receive legal advice and instruct counsel. As well, this procedure provides the accused with an opportunity to purge the contempt: Braun (Trustee of) v. Braun, 2006 ABCA 23 at para 27, 384 AR 80 [Braun]; Rules rr 10.53(3). 34 In Andreachuk, Re (1984), 120 AR 156 at para 15 (CA), the Alberta Court of Appeal held that the judge hearing the contempt application should not be the same judge who issued the order that the accuser seeks to enforce. The reasons are two-fold. First, it prevents any apprehension of bias from arising. Second, this procedure prevents the judge from reading past the literal words of the order that they granted. A different judge, who has not yet seen the order, is in a better position to interpret it impartially. E. — Citing the Person in Contempt: Notice of Contempt and Disclosure of Evidence 35 The accuser must provide the alleged contemnor with specifics of the allegations of contempt, such that the alleged contemnor understands the allegations they face, has an ability to respond to the allegations, and has an opportunity to purge their contempt, if any. If the accuser makes the allegation that the alleged contemnor has breached a court order, the alleged contemnor “must be given an opportunity to provide ‘an adequate excuse’ for his disobedience of a court order”: Metropolitan Life Insurance Co v. Hover (1999), 237 AR 30 at para 6 (CA) [Hover]. 36 In Cotroni v. Quebec Police Commission, [1978] 1 SCR 1048 at 1058 [Cotroni], the Supreme Court of Canada found that where a person was alleged to have committed contempt by providing evasive answers to questions, the accuser should have put the questions that the alleged contemnor failed to answer in the charge. The court in Freedom Villages Inc v. Gander (Town), 2008 NLTD 116 at para 10, 277 Nfld & PEIR 67 [Freedom Villages] states that “the alleged contemnors are entitled to know precisely the charges that are made against them and the evidence by which the charges are to be proven”. 37 Consistent with the disclosure requirements in the criminal context, described in R. v. Stinchcombe, [1991] 3 SCR 326 [Stinchcombe], the alleged contemnor is entitled to be provided with disclosure of the evidence related to the allegations of their contempt. This includes not only that which the accuser intends to rely on, but anything relevant that bears on the alleged contempt itself. This is important as the accuser could be in possession of exculpatory evidence. However, courts must not get too carried away by layering the Stinchcombe requirements on every case in which a party is alleged to have committed civil contempt; each case must be decided on its own facts, and the level of disclosure will depend on those facts. In Vale Inco Ltd v. USW, Local 6500, 2010 ONSC 3039 at para 7, 320 DLR (4th) 185 (Sup Ct) [Vale Inco], Gordon J said: …[T]he nature and extent of the disclosure obligations need to be decided on a case by case basis, having regard to such issues as: (1) The relief being sought by the party bringing the motion for contempt. If the motion is brought essentially for the purpose of ending the unlawful conduct that is one thing; if the motion is brought with a request for significant penal sanction, that is another thing entirely; (2) Whether the alleged contempt is ongoing, resulting in an urgent need to preserve order and protect the authority of the court; (3) If the alleged contempt is not ongoing, whether the relationship between the parties is such that the impugned conduct might reasonably be expected to resume without timely intervention by the court; (4) The nature of the conduct alleged; and (5) The nature and extent of the materials of which disclosure is sought and the time expected to produce it. Gordon J concluded by saying at para 9: It will be important for the court to consider whether the purpose for which disclosure is being sought is legitimate. It will be important for the court to consider whether the ends of justice are best met by making the requested order. 38 The accuser must use Rules Form 27 when it seeks to have a court find the alleged contemnor in contempt. The form asks for particulars of the grounds for making the application and the evidence on which the accuser intends to rely. 39 The alleged contemnor need not answer any allegation that lacks specificity. The alleged contemnor must be provided with a full opportunity to answer and defend the allegation, or to purge the alleged contempt. However, where one allegation fails for a lack of specificity, another, specific, allegation can proceed. F. — Sentencing: Limited Use of Contempt Power 58 Once a court has found the alleged contemnor to be in contempt, it should provide a remedy. In so doing, the court must use the most limited power it has available to achieve the desired objective: United States v. Wilson, 421 US 309 (1975) at 319, cited in K(B) at 197; Arradi at para 33. 59 Recall that the purpose of civil contempt proceedings is coercion rather than punishment: Poje at 517. Consistent with the limited use of the contempt power, and the coercion objective, the Rules give the contemnor the opportunity to purge their contempt. Barring special circumstances, the court should postpone its imposition of a penalty or sanction for a period after it finds the contemnor in contempt, to give the contemnor the opportunity to purge their contempt: Braun at 27. In Braun, the Court noted that the contemnor purging their contempt “may be a mitigating factor” in the imposition of a penalty or sanction. 60 Further, if the court imprisons the contemnor, the imprisonment must end once the contemnor purges their contempt by complying with the order. In In re Armstrong, [1892] 1 QB 327 at 329–330, the court held that the contemnor's imprisonment would end ex debito justitiae, or as of right, when the contemnor “yielded obedience to the order of the Court and paid the costs.” That passage was quoted with approval in Poje at 518 and cited with approval in Cotroni at 1057. Justice Yamauchi also considered the elements of contempt at paragraphs 40-56. The Supreme Court in Carey v. Laiken, 2015 SCC 17, 2015 CarswellOnt 5237, more recently set out the three elements of civil contempt, at paragraphs 32-38: [32] Civil contempt has three elements which must be established beyond a reasonable doubt: Prescott-Russell Services for Children and Adults v. G. (N.) (2006), 2006 CanLII 81792 (ON CA), 82 O.R. (3d) 686 (C.A.), at para. 27; College of Optometrists, at para. 71; Bhatnager v. Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration), 1990 CanLII 120 (SCC), [1990] 2 S.C.R. 217, at pp. 224-25; Jackson v. Honey, 2009 BCCA 112, 267 B.C.A.C. 210, at paras. 12-13; TG Industries Ltd. v. Williams, 2001 NSCA 105, 196 N.S.R. (2d) 35, at paras. 17 and 32; Godin v. Godin, 2012 NSCA 54, 317 N.S.R. (2d) 204, at para. 47; Soper v. Gaudet, 2011 NSCA 11, 298 N.S.R. (2d) 303, at para. 23. These three elements, coupled with the heightened standard of proof, help to ensure that the potential penal consequences of a contempt finding ensue only in appropriate cases: Bell ExpressVu, at para. 22; Chiang, at paras. 10-11. [33] The first element is that the order alleged to have been breached “must state clearly and unequivocally what should and should not be done”: Prescott-Russell, at para. 27; Bell ExpressVu, at para. 28, citing with approval Jaskhs Enterprises Inc. v. Indus Corp., 2004 CanLII 32262 (Ont. S.C.J.), at para. 40. This requirement of clarity ensures that a party will not be found in contempt where an order is unclear: Pro Swing, at para. 24; Bell ExpressVu, at para. 22. An order may be found to be unclear if, for example, it is missing an essential detail about where, when or to whom it applies; if it incorporates overly broad language; or if external circumstances have obscured its meaning: Culligan Canada Ltd. v. Fettes, 2010 SKCA 151, 326 D.L.R. (4th) 463, at para. 21. [34] The second element is that the party alleged to have breached the order must have had actual knowledge of it: Bhatnager, at p. 226; College of Optometrists, at para. 71. It may be possible to infer knowledge in the circumstances, or an alleged contemnor may attract liability on the basis of the wilful blindness doctrine (ibid.). [35] Finally, the party allegedly in breach must have intentionally done the act that the order prohibits or intentionally failed to do the act that the order compels: Sheppard v. Sheppard (1976), 1976 CanLII 710 (ON CA), 12 O.R. (2d) 4 (C.A.), at p. 8. The meaning of this element is one of the main points in contention on appeal and I will turn to consider it in more detail momentarily. [36] The contempt power is discretionary and courts have consistently discouraged its routine use to obtain compliance with court orders: see, e.g., Hefkey v. Hefkey, 2013 ONCA 44, 30 R.F.L. (7th) 65, at para. 3. If contempt is found too easily, “a court's outrage might be treated as just so much bluster that might ultimately cheapen the role and authority of the very judicial power it seeks to protect”: Centre commercial Les Rivières ltée v. Jean Bleu inc., 2012 QCCA 1663, at para. 7. As this Court has affirmed, “contempt of court cannot be reduced to a mere means of enforcing judgments”: Vidéotron Ltée v. Industries Microlec Produits Électroniques Inc., 1992 CanLII 29 (SCC), [1992] 2 S.C.R. 1065, at p. 1078, citing Daigle v. St-Gabriel-de-Brandon (Paroisse), 1991 CanLII 3806 (QC CA), [1991] R.D.J. 249 (Que. C.A.). Rather, it should be used “cautiously and with great restraint”: TG Industries, at para. 32. It is an enforcement power of last rather than first resort: Hefkey, at para. 3; St. Elizabeth Home Society v. Hamilton (City), 2008 ONCA 182, 89 O.R. (3d) 81, at paras. 41-43; Centre commercial Les Rivières ltée, at para. 64. [37] For example, where an alleged contemnor acted in good faith in taking reasonable steps to comply with the order, the judge entertaining a contempt motion generally retains some discretion to decline to make a finding of contempt: see, e.g., Morrow, Power v. Newfoundland Telephone Co. (1994), 1994 CanLII 9723 (NL CA), 121 Nfld. & P.E.I.R. 334 (Nfld. C.A.), at para. 20; TG Industries, at para. 31. While I prefer not to delineate the full scope of this discretion, given that the issue was not argued before us, I wish to leave open the possibility that a judge may properly exercise his or her discretion to decline to impose a contempt finding where it would work an injustice in the circumstances of the case. [38] It is well settled in Canadian common law that all that is required to establish civil contempt is proof beyond a reasonable doubt of an intentional act or omission that is in fact in breach of a clear order of which the alleged contemnor has notice: Prescott-Russell, at para. 27; College of Optometrists, at para. 71; Sheppard, at p. 8; TG Industries, at paras. 17 and 32; Bhatnager, at pp. 224-25; Sharpe, at ¶ 6.190. The Court of Appeal followed this approach. As it noted, to require a contemnor to have intended to disobey the order would put the test “too high” and result in “mistakes of law [becoming] a defence to an allegation of civil contempt but not to a murder charge” (para. 59). Instead, contumacy or lack thereof goes to the penalty to be imposed following a finding of contempt: para. 62; see also Sheppard; and Sharpe, at ¶ 6.200. See also: Koch v. Koch, 2017 ABCA 310, 2017 CarswellAlta 1724, at paragraph 14. The Court of Appeal affirmed Justice Yamauchi's decision in Schitthelm v Kelemen, 2013 ABQB 42, in Alston v. Foothills No. 31 (District of), 2022 ABCA 408, 2022 CarswellAlta 3602. The Court of Appeal said, at paragraph 12: It is no answer to a contempt application that the order was improper or should not have been granted. A court order is valid and enforceable unless and until it is lawfully set aside: Schitthelm v Kelemen, 2013 ABQB 42 at para 44; Builders Energy Services Ltd. v Paddock, 2009 ABCA 153 at para 10. In Porter v. Anytime Custom Mechanical Ltd., 2016 ABQB 322, 2016 CarswellAlta 1096, 60 B.L.R. (5th) 119, Justice Manderscheid gave this summary of the law of contempt: 17 The Supreme Court of Canada in Carey v Laiken, 2015 SCC 17 set out some of the basic principles of civil contempt. First, contempt proceedings are bifurcated into a liability phase and, if liability is established, a penalty phase (para 18). Civil contempt has three elements, each of which must be established beyond a reasonable doubt (para 32): 1. The Order alleged to have been breached must state clearly and unequivocally what should and should not be done (para 33); 2. The alleged contemnor must have had knowledge of the Order (para 34); and 3. The alleged contemnor must have intentionally done the act the Order prohibits or intentionally failed to do the act the Order compels (para 35). 18 In Point on the Bow Development Ltd v William Kelly & Sons Plumbing Contractors Ltd, 2006 ABQB 775, aff'd 2007 ABCA 204, Rooke J (as he then was) discussed these three required elements and added a further qualifier to the third element, based on the language of the Alberta Rules of Court, then R. 703(a) (now r 10.52): “without adequate excuse” (at para 19). 19 Further, the contempt power is discretionary and courts have discouraged its routine use to obtain compliance with a Court order. In Carey, Cromwell J noted (at para 36): If contempt is found too easily, “a court's outrage might be treated as just so much bluster that might ultimately cheapen the role and authority of the very judicial power it seeks to protect”… As this Court has affirmed, “contempt of court cannot be reduced to a mere means of enforcing judgments”: Rather, it should be used “cautiously and with great restraint”… It is an enforcement power of last rather than first resort. (Emphasis added, citations omitted) 20 In regards to intent, the Supreme Court held that all that is necessary is proof beyond a reasonable doubt of the intentional act or omission that is a clear breach of the Order; an intent to disobey the Order is not necessary. Contumacy, or lack of it, goes to the penalty phase of the hearing (para 38). However, a respondent will not be held in contempt for breach of an implied or inferred term in an order, since the Order must be clear, precise and unambiguous, and further the alleged contemnor is entitled to the most favourable interpretation of the order: Milne v Milne, 2014 BCSC 2423 (at para 57 and 47). 21 An Order for contempt is a final order and therefore hearsay is not admissible: Letal v Lakeland Roman Catholic Separate School District N. 150, 2000 ABQB 801 (at para 17); Kulyk v Wigmore, 1987 ABCA 127, 53 Alta LR (2d) 44 (CA) (at para 3). See also Kadar v. 720294 Alberta Corp, 2002 ABQB 1019 (at para 21); Bee Chemical Co v Plastic Paint & Finish Specialties Ltd (1979), 47 CPR (2d) 172 (Ont. CA) (at para 9); Krien v Krien, [1997] BCJ No. 643 (BCSC). Further, contempt applications are matters of strictissim juris (Letal at para 32) and contempt allegations are serious and quasi-criminal, therefore procedural fairness is essential (Brown v Arès, 2005 ABCA 438, at para 5; Kadar at para 21; Continuing Care Employers' Bargaining Association v AUPE, 2002 ABCA 148, 303 AR 137 (CA)). 22 In Arrow-West Equipment Ltd v GDT Trading Ltd, 2006 ABQB 762, Acton J noted that the particulars of alleged contempt must be sufficient to put the respondents on notice as to the alleged grounds (para 30). General allegations are not sufficient and the Respondents must not be left to guess at the specifics of the matters complained of. In 473440 Alberta Ltd. v. Lenaco Homes Masterbuilder Inc., 2017 ABQB 538, 2017 CarswellAlta 1610, Justice Feehan gave this summary of the law: 44 Courts have inherent jurisdiction to deal with contempt of their orders. In the leading case on the common law test for civil contempt, Carey v Laiken, 2015 SCC 17, [2015] 2 SCR 79, the Supreme Court endorsed the following principles: • contempt of court rests on the power of the court to uphold its dignity and process, and the rule of law directly depends on the ability of the courts to enforce their process and maintain their dignity and respect: para 30; • the purpose of a contempt order is first and foremost a declaration that a party has acted in defiance of a court order: para 30; • use of the contempt power is discretionary; it should be used cautiously and with great restraint, not to obtain routine compliance with court orders nor as a mere means of enforcing judgments; it is an enforcement power of last rather than first resort: paras 31 & 36; • contempt proceedings are bifurcated to address first liability and then penalty: para 18; • in order to establish liability, each of the following three elements of civil contempt must be established beyond a reasonable doubt, para 32: 1. the order alleged to have been breached must state clearly and unequivocally what should and should not be done; for example, an order may be found to be unclear if it is missing an essential detail about where, when or to whom it applies, if it incorporates overly broad language, or if external circumstances have obscured its meaning: para 33; 2. the alleged contemnor must have had actual, or inferred, knowledge of it or have been wilfully blind to the order: para 34; and 3. the alleged contemnor must have intentionally done the act that the order prohibits, or intentionally failed to do the act that the order compels; it is not necessary that the alleged contemnor intended to disobey the order; “contumacy”[perverse and obstinate resistance or disobedience] goes to penalty rather than liability; the alleged contemnor cannot rely on a misinterpretation of a clear order or legal advice to shield it from a contempt finding; similarly, lawyers cannot rely on their own legal advice as a shield: paras 35, 38, 42 & 44. 45 The Supreme Court in Carey confirmed prior law to the effect that the mens rea required is only an intention to commit the prohibited act or the intentional, wilful or reckless failure to perform the required act: Precision Forest Industries v Cox, 2013 ABQB 524, [2013] A.J. No. 1000 at para 41. 46 Rooke J. (as he then was) in Point on the Bow Development Ltd v Kelly (William) & Sons Plumbing Contractors Ltd, 2006 ABQB 775 at para 21, 405 AR 1 noted that while the act that constitutes contempt must be intentional, rather than accidental, neither a general intent to do the act forbidden nor a specific intent to disobey is required. See also Michel v LaFrentz, 1998 ABCA 231, [1998] A.J. No. 1489 at para 24; Saunders v Saunders, 2017 ABQB 163, [2017] A.J. No. 222 at para 11; Broda v Broda, 2004 ABCA 72, [2004] A.J. No. 180 at para 7; FIC Real Estate Fund Ltd v Lennie, 2014 ABQB 105, [2014] A.J. No 184 at paras 82 & 83; 2363523 Ontario Inc v Nowack, 2016 ONCA 951, [2016] O.J. No. 6508 at para 24. 47 Sloppy and unacceptable practice, without more, does not amount to contempt: Miller v 32807 Alberta Ltd (1986), 70 AR 303, [1986] A.J. No. 407 at para 3 (CA); Precision Forest Industries at para 31; Jutte v Jutte, 2007 ABQB 191, [2007] A.J. No. 426 at para 44. 48 In Alberta, Rule 10.52(3) additionally provides:
paragraphs.heading: Part 10. Lawyers' Charges, Recoverable Costs Of Litigation, And Sanctions

sentences.text: Commentary § 10.52:1 Rule 10.52 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta.
Reg.
In Schitthelm v.
Kelemen, 2013 ABQB 42, 2013 CarswellAlta 239, 557 A.R.
(2d) 235, Justice Yamauchi provided a comprehensive summary of the law regarding contempt.
His Lordship said: B. — The Nature of the Contempt Power 19 Superior courts have the inherent jurisdiction to control the proceedings before them.
For a court to operate effectively, it requires an ability to maintain order in its proceedings and ensure its directions are followed.
This is part of the rule of law.
20 Courts have differentiated between contempt of a civil nature and contempt of a criminal nature: see e.g.
Poje v.
British Columbia (Attorney General), [1953] 1 SCR 516 at 517 [Poje]; United Nurses of Alberta v.
Alberta (Attorney General), [1992] 1 SCR 901 at 931 [United Nurses]; Chiang (Trustee of) v.
Chiang, 2009 ONCA 3 at para 10, 93 OR (3d) 483 and Seaward v.
However, in Vidéotron Ltée v.

Industries Microlec Products Électioniques Inc, [1992] 2 SCR 1065 at 1075 [Vidéotron], Gonthier J warns that “too great an insistence on the distinction between civil contempt and criminal contempt” could mask characteristics common to all types of contempt.
In Pro Swing Inc v.

Elta Golf Inc, 2006 SCC 52 at para 34, [2006] 2 SCR 612 [Pro Swing], the Supreme Court of Canada states that the decision in Vidéotron set “aside the distinction between the civil and criminal aspects” of contempt law.
Why is this?
As mentioned in R. v.
Cohn

(2d) 65 at para 11 [Cohn]: … the [Criminal] Code does not specifically provide for or define any such offence nor does it set forth any procedure for the prosecution of such offence or any penalty following conviction therefor.
Resort must be had to the common law for these matters.
Contempt of court is a common law offence.
Thus, contempt, whether of a criminal or civil nature derives from the same source, the common law.

Certainly, the context in which each occurs might differ, and the results that flow from each might inform whether the contempt is “civil” or “criminal.” However, as noted in Halsbury's Laws of England, vol 22, 5th ed (London, UK: LexisNexis, 2012) at para 2, footnote 1 [citations omitted], “[t]he classification of contempts as criminal or civil has become progressively less important and has been described as ‘unhelpful and almost meaningless’ in the present day”.

21 Vidéotron and Pro Swing indicate that contempt should not be looked at as merely “civil or “criminal” in nature, because all contempt has a public aspect and is of a “quasi-criminal nature”: Pro Swing at para 36.

22 While courts have held that civil contempt is generally coercive in nature and criminal contempt punitive in nature, this Court is not convinced that the procedural rights that attach to contempt proceedings and the Charter's applicability to them change merely because of the way in which one classifies the contempt.
In all cases, courts must examine the particular facts before them and determine the procedures that natural justice and the Charter require.
C. — Charter Applicability 23 The Charter is engaged when a person's liberty is at risk: see e.g.
Re BC Motor Vehicle Act, [1985] 2 SCR 486.
In a contempt application, a person's liberty may be at risk: Rules rr 10.53(1)(a)–(c).

Is the Charter engaged when a person faces a finding that they are in civil contempt pursuant to the Rules? … 25 Has a person who is alleged to have committed civil contempt been “charged” with anything?
In Cohn at 75–76, the Ontario Court of Appeal said: The heading which precedes s.
11 of the Charter reads: “Proceedings in criminal and penal matters”.
The portion of s.
11 which determines in the first instance the persons who may derive the benefit thereof is the first line which states: “Any person charged with an offence has the right …”.
The heading to s.
11 makes it clear that s.
11 of the Charter applies to an offence although it may not be, strictly speaking, a criminal matter.
It is sufficient if it is a penal matter.
Even if contempt proceedings are not properly characterized as criminal matters, there can be no doubt that they must, at the very least, be characterized as penal matters.
The word “penal” as used in the heading undoubtedly bears the dictionary meaning “of, pertaining to or relating to punishment”.
It is the power to punish for contempt of court which is expressly preserved by s.
8 of the Criminal Code and, as previously stated, I am of the view that the citation for contempt of court constitutes the charging of an offence within the meaning of s.
It follows, therefore, that s.
11(c) and (d) of the Charter are applicable to contempt of court proceedings.

26 While one might think that, in a civil matter, the party making the application to have the court find the other party in civil contempt simply wants to have the court order enforced for its benefit, there can be no doubt that Rules rr 10.53(1)(b) and 10.53(1)(c) are penal in nature.
The spectre of that punishment alone makes the Rules that govern civil contempt subject to the Charter, or at least some of its provisions.
See e.g.
R. v.
Winter (1986), 72 AR 164 at para 9 [Winter], where the Alberta Court of Appeal chose not to follow a decision of the Québec Superior Court in Attorney-General of Quebec v.
Laurendeau (1982), 3 CCC (3d) 250, which held that a person cited for contempt was not “charged” with an offence within the meaning of Charter s 11.
In Placentia-St.
Mary's Roman Catholic School Board v.
Newfoundland Association of Public Employees, Local 5802

(1986), 60 Nfld & PEIR 350 at para 4 (Nfld SC (TD)), Steele J said “[t]he penalty for contempt of court may involve a fine or committal to jail and is therefore a punishment affecting the liberty of the person.

Consequently contempt proceedings may have definite overtones of a criminal nature.” At paragraph 5, Steele J went on to quote, with agreement, the following passage from Nigel Lowe & Sir Gordon Borrie, Borrie & Lowe's Law of Contempt, 2nd ed (London, UK: Butterworths, 1983) at 393, where the authors said: Although this aspect of contempt is designated civil, because of the penal sanctions, it has been said to “partake of a criminal nature” and many of the rules that normally apply when seeking to prove an accused guilty of a crime, apply when seeking to show that the defendant has committed civil contempt.
It also means that the rules safeguarding contemners'[sic] rights must be strictly complied with.
[Footnotes omitted.] 27 Even if one concedes that Charter rights are engaged, does this provide a complete answer to the question concerning the procedures a court must use in contempt proceedings?
The Charter itself comes with built-in limits.
Charter s 7 provides that every right contained in that section is subject to restrictions that are in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice.

As well, every Charter right can be limited by engaging Charter s 1, which provides for “such reasonable limits prescribed by law as can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society.” Indeed, in Winter at para 12, the Alberta Court of Appeal found the instanter procedure which the trial judge used to find the accused in contempt was justified under Charter s.
28 In a civil contempt proceeding, the court may not discard the alleged contemnor's rights.
The court must, however, carefully balance those rights against those of the party who alleges that the alleged contemnor has committed civil contempt.

Above all, when a court considers the procedural requirements that are engaged in a civil contempt proceeding, it must ensure that the alleged contemnor is not found to have committed contempt without adequate proof of culpability.
This informs all aspects of contempt procedure.
29 The procedure required to address the competing interests in contempt applications will not always remain constant; each case depends on its particular facts.
D. — Procedure 30 In R. v.

K(B), [1995] 4 SCR 186 at para 11 [K(B)], Lamer CJ said: In order to simplify matters, it is my opinion that we should use the notion of citing in contempt, not as an expression of a finding of contempt but instead, as a method of providing the accused with notice that he or she has been contemptuous and will be required to show cause why they should not be held in contempt.

31 While the cases that deal with criminal contempt are distinguishable from civil contempt under the Rules, they are instructive in assisting the courts in fashioning a procedure to use when considering an allegation of civil contempt.
What emerges from those cases, and what natural justice and the Charter require, is a three-stage procedure: citing the person in contempt of the court, conviction and sentencing.

Under the Rules, those stages are specifically outlined as follows: Citing the person in contempt of the court: Rules rr 10.52(1) and 10.52(2) require the accuser provide the alleged contemnor with notice of the application for a declaration of civil contempt
Conviction: Rules r 10.52(3) allows the judge to “declare” the alleged contemnor to be in civil contempt
Sentencing: Rules r 10.53 outlines the “penalties” and “sanctions” the judge might impose on the contemnor.
32 Each stage should be separated, unless there is an urgent and imperative reason why the stages should be collapsed so the procedure can be expedited: R. v.
Arradi, 2003 SCC 23 at para 30, [2003] 1 SCR 280 [Arradi]; Doobay v.
Diamond, 2012 ONCA 580 at para 40, leave to appeal to SCC requested.

As well, the Rules provide that a judge may cite and declare the person to be in contempt instanter in appropriate circumstances: Winter. … 33 Except in the case of a judge using an instanter summary procedure, this procedure allows, among other things, the alleged contemnor to receive legal advice and instruct counsel.
As well, this procedure provides the accused with an opportunity to purge the contempt: Braun (Trustee of) v.
Braun, 2006 ABCA 23 at para 27, 384 AR 80 [Braun]; Rules rr 10.53(3).

34 In Andreachuk, Re (1984), 120 AR 156 at para 15 (CA), the Alberta Court of Appeal held that the judge hearing the contempt application should not be the same judge who issued the order that the accuser seeks to enforce.
The reasons are two-fold.
First, it prevents any apprehension of bias from arising.
Second, this procedure prevents the judge from reading past the literal words of the order that they granted.
A different judge, who has not yet seen the order, is in a better position to interpret it impartially.

E. — Citing the Person in Contempt: Notice of Contempt and Disclosure of Evidence 35 The accuser must provide the alleged contemnor with specifics of the allegations of contempt, such that the alleged contemnor understands the allegations they face, has an ability to respond to the allegations, and has an opportunity to purge their contempt, if any.

If the accuser makes the allegation that the alleged contemnor has breached a court order, the alleged contemnor “must be given an opportunity to provide ‘an adequate excuse’ for his disobedience of a court order”: Metropolitan Life Insurance Co v.
Hover (1999), 237 AR 30 at para 6 (CA) [Hover].
36 In Cotroni v.

Quebec Police Commission, [1978] 1 SCR 1048 at 1058 [Cotroni], the Supreme Court of Canada found that where a person was alleged to have committed contempt by providing evasive answers to questions, the accuser should have put the questions that the alleged contemnor failed to answer in the charge.
The court in Freedom Villages Inc v.

Gander (Town), 2008 NLTD 116 at para 10, 277 Nfld & PEIR 67 [Freedom Villages] states that “the alleged contemnors are entitled to know precisely the charges that are made against them and the evidence by which the charges are to be proven”.
37 Consistent with the disclosure requirements in the criminal context, described in R. v.
Stinchcombe, [1991] 3 SCR 326 [Stinchcombe], the alleged contemnor is entitled to be provided with disclosure of the evidence related to the allegations of their contempt.
This includes not only that which the accuser intends to rely on, but anything relevant that bears on the alleged contempt itself.
This is important as the accuser could be in possession of exculpatory evidence.

However, courts must not get too carried away by layering the Stinchcombe requirements on every case in which a party is alleged to have committed civil contempt; each case must be decided on its own facts, and the level of disclosure will depend on those facts.
In Vale Inco Ltd v.
USW, Local 6500, 2010 ONSC 3039 at para 7, 320 DLR
(4th) 185 (Sup Ct) [Vale Inco], Gordon J said: …[T]he nature and extent of the disclosure obligations need to be decided on a case by case basis, having regard to such issues as:
(1) The relief being sought by the party bringing the motion for contempt.

If the motion is brought essentially for the purpose of ending the unlawful conduct that is one thing; if the motion is brought with a request for significant penal sanction, that is another thing entirely
(2) Whether the alleged contempt is ongoing, resulting in an urgent need to preserve order and protect the authority of the court

(3) If the alleged contempt is not ongoing, whether the relationship between the parties is such that the impugned conduct might reasonably be expected to resume without timely intervention by the court
(4) The nature of the conduct alleged; and
(5) The nature and extent of the materials of which disclosure is sought and the time expected to produce it.
Gordon J concluded by saying at para 9: It will be important for the court to consider whether the purpose for which disclosure is being sought is legitimate.
It will be important for the court to consider whether the ends of justice are best met by making the requested order.
38 The accuser must use Rules Form 27 when it seeks to have a court find the alleged contemnor in contempt.
The form asks for particulars of the grounds for making the application and the evidence on which the accuser intends to rely.
39 The alleged contemnor need not answer any allegation that lacks specificity.
The alleged contemnor must be provided with a full opportunity to answer and defend the allegation, or to purge the alleged contempt.
However, where one allegation fails for a lack of specificity, another, specific, allegation can proceed.
F. — Sentencing: Limited Use of Contempt Power 58 Once a court has found the alleged contemnor to be in contempt, it should provide a remedy.
In so doing, the court must use the most limited power it has available to achieve the desired objective: United States v.
Wilson, 421 US 309 (1975) at 319, cited in K(B) at 197; Arradi at para 33.
59 Recall that the purpose of civil contempt proceedings is coercion rather than punishment: Poje at 517.
Consistent with the limited use of the contempt power, and the coercion objective, the Rules give the contemnor the opportunity to purge their contempt.

Barring special circumstances, the court should postpone its imposition of a penalty or sanction for a period after it finds the contemnor in contempt, to give the contemnor the opportunity to purge their contempt: Braun at 27.
In Braun, the Court noted that the contemnor purging their contempt “may be a mitigating factor” in the imposition of a penalty or sanction.
60 Further, if the court imprisons the contemnor, the imprisonment must end once the contemnor purges their contempt by complying with the order.

In In re Armstrong, [1892] 1 QB 327 at 329–330, the court held that the contemnor's imprisonment would end ex debito justitiae, or as of right, when the contemnor “yielded obedience to the order of the Court and paid the costs.” That passage was quoted with approval in Poje at 518 and cited with approval in Cotroni at 1057.
Justice Yamauchi also considered the elements of contempt at paragraphs 40-56.
The Supreme Court in Carey v.

Laiken, 2015 SCC 17, 2015 CarswellOnt 5237, more recently set out the three elements of civil contempt, at paragraphs 32-38: [32] Civil contempt has three elements which must be established beyond a reasonable doubt: Prescott-Russell Services for Children and Adults v.
G.
(3d) 686 (C.A.), at para.
27; College of Optometrists, at para.
71; Bhatnager v.
Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration), 1990 CanLII 120 (SCC), [1990] 2 S.C.R.
217, at pp.
224-25; Jackson v.
Honey, 2009 BCCA 112, 267 B.C.A.C.
210, at paras.
12-13; TG Industries Ltd. v.
Williams, 2001 NSCA 105, 196 N.S.R.
(2d) 35, at paras.
17 and 32; Godin v.
Godin, 2012 NSCA 54, 317 N.S.R.
(2d) 204, at para.
47; Soper v.
Gaudet, 2011 NSCA 11, 298 N.S.R.
(2d) 303, at para.

These three elements, coupled with the heightened standard of proof, help to ensure that the potential penal consequences of a contempt finding ensue only in appropriate cases: Bell ExpressVu, at para.
22; Chiang, at paras.
[33] The first element is that the order alleged to have been breached “must state clearly and unequivocally what should and should not be done”: Prescott-Russell, at para.
27; Bell ExpressVu, at para.
28, citing with approval Jaskhs Enterprises Inc. v.
Indus Corp., 2004 CanLII 32262 (Ont.
S.C.J.), at para.
This requirement of clarity ensures that a party will not be found in contempt where an order is unclear: Pro Swing, at para.
24; Bell ExpressVu, at para.

An order may be found to be unclear if, for example, it is missing an essential detail about where, when or to whom it applies; if it incorporates overly broad language; or if external circumstances have obscured its meaning: Culligan Canada Ltd. v.
Fettes, 2010 SKCA 151, 326 D.L.R.
(4th) 463, at para.
[34] The second element is that the party alleged to have breached the order must have had actual knowledge of it: Bhatnager, at p.
226; College of Optometrists, at para.
It may be possible to infer knowledge in the circumstances, or an alleged contemnor may attract liability on the basis of the wilful blindness doctrine (ibid.).
[35] Finally, the party allegedly in breach must have intentionally done the act that the order prohibits or intentionally failed to do the act that the order compels: Sheppard v.
Sheppard (1976), 1976 CanLII 710 (ON CA), 12 O.R.
The meaning of this element is one of the main points in contention on appeal and I will turn to consider it in more detail momentarily.
[36] The contempt power is discretionary and courts have consistently discouraged its routine use to obtain compliance with court orders: see, e.g., Hefkey v.
Hefkey, 2013 ONCA 44, 30 R.F.L.
(7th) 65, at para.

If contempt is found too easily, “a court's outrage might be treated as just so much bluster that might ultimately cheapen the role and authority of the very judicial power it seeks to protect”: Centre commercial Les Rivières ltée v.
Jean Bleu inc., 2012 QCCA 1663, at para.
As this Court has affirmed, “contempt of court cannot be reduced to a mere means of enforcing judgments”: Vidéotron Ltée v.
Industries Microlec Produits Électroniques Inc., 1992 CanLII 29 (SCC), [1992] 2 S.C.R.
1078, citing Daigle v.
St-Gabriel-de-Brandon (Paroisse), 1991 CanLII 3806 (QC CA), [1991] R.D.J.
Rather, it should be used “cautiously and with great restraint”: TG Industries, at para.
It is an enforcement power of last rather than first resort: Hefkey, at para.
3; St.
Elizabeth Home Society v.
Hamilton (City), 2008 ONCA 182, 89 O.R.
(3d) 81, at paras.
41-43; Centre commercial Les Rivières ltée, at para.

[37] For example, where an alleged contemnor acted in good faith in taking reasonable steps to comply with the order, the judge entertaining a contempt motion generally retains some discretion to decline to make a finding of contempt: see, e.g., Morrow, Power v.
Newfoundland Telephone Co.
(1994), 1994 CanLII 9723 (NL CA), 121 Nfld. & P.E.I.R.
334 (Nfld.
C.A.), at para.
20; TG Industries, at para.

While I prefer not to delineate the full scope of this discretion, given that the issue was not argued before us, I wish to leave open the possibility that a judge may properly exercise his or her discretion to decline to impose a contempt finding where it would work an injustice in the circumstances of the case.

[38] It is well settled in Canadian common law that all that is required to establish civil contempt is proof beyond a reasonable doubt of an intentional act or omission that is in fact in breach of a clear order of which the alleged contemnor has notice: Prescott-Russell, at para.
27; College of Optometrists, at para.
71; Sheppard, at p.
8; TG Industries, at paras.
17 and 32; Bhatnager, at pp.
The Court of Appeal followed this approach.

As it noted, to require a contemnor to have intended to disobey the order would put the test “too high” and result in “mistakes of law [becoming] a defence to an allegation of civil contempt but not to a murder charge” (para.
Instead, contumacy or lack thereof goes to the penalty to be imposed following a finding of contempt: para.
62; see also Sheppard; and Sharpe, at ¶ 6.200.
See also: Koch v.
Koch, 2017 ABCA 310, 2017 CarswellAlta 1724, at paragraph 14.
The Court of Appeal affirmed Justice Yamauchi's decision in Schitthelm v Kelemen, 2013 ABQB 42, in Alston v.
Foothills No.
31 (District of), 2022 ABCA 408, 2022 CarswellAlta 3602.
The Court of Appeal said, at paragraph 12: It is no answer to a contempt application that the order was improper or should not have been granted.
A court order is valid and enforceable unless and until it is lawfully set aside: Schitthelm v Kelemen, 2013 ABQB 42 at para 44; Builders Energy Services Ltd. v Paddock, 2009 ABCA 153 at para 10.
In Porter v.
Anytime Custom Mechanical Ltd., 2016 ABQB 322, 2016 CarswellAlta 1096, 60 B.L.R.
(5th) 119, Justice Manderscheid gave this summary of the law of contempt: 17 The Supreme Court of Canada in Carey v Laiken, 2015 SCC 17 set out some of the basic principles of civil contempt.
First, contempt proceedings are bifurcated into a liability phase and, if liability is established, a penalty phase (para 18).
Civil contempt has three elements, each of which must be established beyond a reasonable doubt (para 32): 1.
The Order alleged to have been breached must state clearly and unequivocally what should and should not be done (para 33); 2.
The alleged contemnor must have had knowledge of the Order (para 34); and 3.
The alleged contemnor must have intentionally done the act the Order prohibits or intentionally failed to do the act the Order compels (para 35).

18 In Point on the Bow Development Ltd v William Kelly & Sons Plumbing Contractors Ltd, 2006 ABQB 775, aff'd 2007 ABCA 204, Rooke J (as he then was) discussed these three required elements and added a further qualifier to the third element, based on the language of the Alberta Rules of Court, then R.
703(a) (now r 10.52): “without adequate excuse” (at para 19).
19 Further, the contempt power is discretionary and courts have discouraged its routine use to obtain compliance with a Court order.

In Carey, Cromwell J noted (at para 36): If contempt is found too easily, “a court's outrage might be treated as just so much bluster that might ultimately cheapen the role and authority of the very judicial power it seeks to protect”… As this Court has affirmed, “contempt of court cannot be reduced to a mere means of enforcing judgments”: Rather, it should be used “cautiously and with great restraint”… It is an enforcement power of last rather than first resort.

(Emphasis added, citations omitted) 20 In regards to intent, the Supreme Court held that all that is necessary is proof beyond a reasonable doubt of the intentional act or omission that is a clear breach of the Order; an intent to disobey the Order is not necessary.
Contumacy, or lack of it, goes to the penalty phase of the hearing (para 38).

However, a respondent will not be held in contempt for breach of an implied or inferred term in an order, since the Order must be clear, precise and unambiguous, and further the alleged contemnor is entitled to the most favourable interpretation of the order: Milne v Milne, 2014 BCSC 2423 (at para 57 and 47).
21 An Order for contempt is a final order and therefore hearsay is not admissible: Letal v Lakeland Roman Catholic Separate School District N.
150, 2000 ABQB 801 (at para 17); Kulyk v Wigmore, 1987 ABCA 127, 53 Alta LR (2d) 44 (CA) (at para 3).
See also Kadar v.
720294 Alberta Corp, 2002 ABQB 1019 (at para 21); Bee Chemical Co v Plastic Paint & Finish Specialties Ltd (1979), 47 CPR (2d) 172 (Ont.
CA) (at para 9); Krien v Krien, [1997] BCJ No.
643 (BCSC).

Further, contempt applications are matters of strictissim juris (Letal at para 32) and contempt allegations are serious and quasi-criminal, therefore procedural fairness is essential (Brown v Arès, 2005 ABCA 438, at para 5
Kadar at para 21
Continuing Care Employers' Bargaining Association v AUPE, 2002 ABCA 148, 303 AR 137 (CA)).

22 In Arrow-West Equipment Ltd v GDT Trading Ltd, 2006 ABQB 762, Acton J noted that the particulars of alleged contempt must be sufficient to put the respondents on notice as to the alleged grounds (para 30).
General allegations are not sufficient and the Respondents must not be left to guess at the specifics of the matters complained of.
In 473440 Alberta Ltd. v.
Lenaco Homes Masterbuilder Inc., 2017 ABQB 538, 2017 CarswellAlta 1610, Justice Feehan gave this summary of the law: 44 Courts have inherent jurisdiction to deal with contempt of their orders.

In the leading case on the common law test for civil contempt, Carey v Laiken, 2015 SCC 17, [2015] 2 SCR 79, the Supreme Court endorsed the following principles: • contempt of court rests on the power of the court to uphold its dignity and process, and the rule of law directly depends on the ability of the courts to enforce their process and maintain their dignity and respect: para 30; • the purpose of a contempt order is first and foremost a declaration that a party has acted in defiance of a court order: para 30; • use of the contempt power is discretionary; it should be used cautiously and with great restraint, not to obtain routine compliance with court orders nor as a mere means of enforcing judgments; it is an enforcement power of last rather than first resort: paras 31 & 36; • contempt proceedings are bifurcated to address first liability and then penalty: para 18; • in order to establish liability, each of the following three elements of civil contempt must be established beyond a reasonable doubt, para 32: 1. the order alleged to have been breached must state clearly and unequivocally what should and should not be done; for example, an order may be found to be unclear if it is missing an essential detail about where, when or to whom it applies, if it incorporates overly broad language, or if external circumstances have obscured its meaning: para 33; 2. the alleged contemnor must have had actual, or inferred, knowledge of it or have been wilfully blind to the order: para 34; and 3. the alleged contemnor must have intentionally done the act that the order prohibits, or intentionally failed to do the act that the order compels; it is not necessary that the alleged contemnor intended to disobey the order; “contumacy”[perverse and obstinate resistance or disobedience] goes to penalty rather than liability; the alleged contemnor cannot rely on a misinterpretation of a clear order or legal advice to shield it from a contempt finding; similarly, lawyers cannot rely on their own legal advice as a shield: paras 35, 38, 42 & 44.

45 The Supreme Court in Carey confirmed prior law to the effect that the mens rea required is only an intention to commit the prohibited act or the intentional, wilful or reckless failure to perform the required act: Precision Forest Industries v Cox, 2013 ABQB 524, [2013] A.J.
No.
1000 at para 41.
46 Rooke J.

(as he then was) in Point on the Bow Development Ltd v Kelly (William) & Sons Plumbing Contractors Ltd, 2006 ABQB 775 at para 21, 405 AR 1 noted that while the act that constitutes contempt must be intentional, rather than accidental, neither a general intent to do the act forbidden nor a specific intent to disobey is required.
See also Michel v LaFrentz, 1998 ABCA 231, [1998] A.J.
No.
1489 at para 24; Saunders v Saunders, 2017 ABQB 163, [2017] A.J.
No.
222 at para 11; Broda v Broda, 2004 ABCA 72, [2004] A.J.
No.
180 at para 7; FIC Real Estate Fund Ltd v Lennie, 2014 ABQB 105, [2014] A.J.
No 184 at paras 82 & 83; 2363523 Ontario Inc v Nowack, 2016 ONCA 951, [2016] O.J.
No.
6508 at para 24.
47 Sloppy and unacceptable practice, without more, does not amount to contempt: Miller v 32807 Alberta Ltd (1986), 70 AR 303, [1986] A.J.
No.
407 at para 3 (CA); Precision Forest Industries at para 31; Jutte v Jutte, 2007 ABQB 191, [2007] A.J.
No.
426 at para 44.
48 In Alberta, Rule 10.52(3) additionally provides:

paragraphs.heading: Part 10. Lawyers' Charges, Recoverable Costs Of Litigation, And Sanctions

paragraphs.section_heading: Rule 10.52 – Part 10. Lawyers' Charges, Recoverable Costs Of Litigation, And Sanctions
paragraphs.text: (3) A judge may declare a person to be in civil contempt of Court if (a) the person, without reasonable excuse, (i) does not comply with an order … of which the person has actual knowledge. … [Emphasis added] 49 There is a difference of opinion in the case law as to the onus in relation to reasonable excuse. Rules 10.51 and 10.52 contemplate that the alleged contemnor will appear to “show cause” why that person should not be declared to be in civil contempt. That begs the question as to what, if any, onus lies on the alleged contemnor in relation to a reasonable excuse. 50 In Schitthelm v Kelemen, 2013 ABQB 42, [2013] A.J. Types of Contempt and Powers in Relation Thereto (i)—Civil contempt At the outset I propose to make some general remarks concerning contempt of Court so that others besides those appearing here today will have a more precise knowledge of what consequence can flow from the disobedience of lawful orders of the Supreme Court of this or any other Province in this country. That disobedience may amount to civil contempt or criminal contempt. The parties to a civil action, such as here, can apply on motion for an order for civil contempt where an order of the Court has not been obeyed. Our Rules of Court set out the penalties that may be imposed for civil contempt. Those penalties are set forth in Rule 704. It says: 704. Every person in civil contempt is liable to any one or more of the following: (a) imprisonment until he has purged his contempt; (b) imprisonment for one year; (c) a fine of $1,000 and in default of payment thereof, to imprisonment for one year; and other sanctions such as striking out pleadings. (ii)—Criminal contempt But the Criminal Code of Canada contains a provision, s. 116, which also covers the situation. Section 116 of the Criminal Code says: 116. Every one who, without lawful excuse, disobeys a lawful order made by a court of justice or by a person or body of persons authorized by any Act to make or give the order, other than an order for the payment of money is, unless some penalty or punishment or other mode of proceeding is expressly provided by law, guilty of (a) an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for two years; or (b) an offence punishable on summary conviction. All that means is that the Attorney-General of this Province or any other Province, being the chief law enforcement officer, can prefer an indictment against people who disobey lawful orders of the Court. The Court may ex mero motu, that is of its motion, institute proceedings for criminal contempt and this contempt, if confirmed, permits penalties that are virtually unlimited. And that power has come down through the ages and rests in every Court of superior jurisdiction. So it would be folly for any one to assume that contempt proceedings depend on the parties to the action or that one must await the application of the Attorney-General. The inherent power of the Court to institute contempt proceedings is always there and it does not only reside in the justice of the Court whose order has been disobeyed. Any member of the Supreme Court of Alberta may, of his own motion, institute such proceedings, and at this moment with the evidence before me and the admissions before me I have the power to change these proceedings from civil contempt to one of criminal contempt, and if I do that and if criminal contempt is found, I will also have the power as a member of this Court to impose virtually any penalty. Criminal versus Civil Contempt It is my view that a clear distinction exists between civil and criminal contempt and that the law of criminal contempt is sufficiently certain to meet the requirements of fundamental justice. The distinction between civil and criminal contempt rests in the concept of public defiance that accompanies criminal contempt. Both civil and criminal contempt of court rest on the power of the court to uphold its dignity and process. The rule of law is at the heart of our society; without it there can be neither peace, nor order nor good government. The rule of law is directly dependent on the ability of the courts to enforce their process and maintain their dignity and respect. To maintain their process and respect, courts since the 12th century have exercised the power to punish for contempt of court. These same courts found it necessary to distinguish between civil and criminal contempt. A person who simply breaches a court order, for example by failing to abide by visiting hours stipulated in a child custody order, is viewed as having committed civil contempt. However, when the element of public defiance of the court's process in a way calculated to lessen societal respect for the courts is added to the breach, it becomes criminal. This distinction emerges from Poje v. Attorney General for British Columbia, [1953] 1 S.C.R. 516, at p. 527, per Kellock J.: The context in which these incidents occurred, the large numbers of men involved and the public nature of the defiance of the order of the court transfer the conduct here in question from the realm of a mere civil contempt, such as an ordinary breach of injunction with respect to private rights in a patent or trade-mark, for example, into the realm of a public depreciation of the authority of the court tending to bring the administration of justice into scorn. [Emphasis added by McLachlin J.] What the courts have fastened on in this and other cases where criminal contempt has been found is the concept of public defiance that “transcends the limits of any dispute between particular litigants and constitutes an affront to the administration of justice as a whole”: B.C.G.E.U. v. British Columbia (Attorney General), supra, at p. 237, per Dickson C.J., Lamer, Wilson, La Forest, and L'Heureux-Dubé JJ. concurring. The gravamen of the offence is not actual or threatened injury to persons or property; other offences deal with those evils. The gravamen of the offence is rather the open, continuous and flagrant violation of a court order without regard for the effect that may have on the respect accorded to edicts of the court. U.N.A. v. Alberta (Attorney General), [1992] 1 S.C.R. 901, at 931–32, per McLachlin J. for the majority. In R. v. Edmonton Sun (2003), 12 Alta. L.R. (4th) 6 (C.A.), McFadyen J.A. said at p. 19: Criminal contempt is, therefore, clearly aimed at punishing public acts which tend to bring the administration of justice into disrepute and interfere with the due administration of justice. 6. Requirements to Prove Criminal Contempt To establish criminal contempt the Crown must prove that the accused defied or disobeyed a court order in a public way (the actus reus), with intent, knowledge or recklessness as to the fact that the public disobedience will tend to depreciate the authority of the court (the mens rea). The Crown must prove these elements beyond a reasonable doubt. As in other criminal offences, however, the necessary mens rea may be inferred from the circumstances. An open and public defiance of a court order will tend to depreciate the authority of the court. Therefore when it is clear the accused must have known his or her act of defiance will be public, it may be inferred that he or she was at least reckless as to whether the authority of the court would be brought into contempt. On the other hand, if the circumstances leave a reasonable doubt as to whether the breach was or should be expected to have this public quality, then the necessary mens rea would not be present and the accused would be acquitted, even if the matter in fact became public. While publicity is required for the offence, a civil contempt is not converted to a criminal contempt merely because it attracts publicity, as the union contends, but rather because it constitutes a public act of defiance of the court in circumstances where the accused knew, intended or was reckless as to the fact that the act would publicly bring the court into contempt. U.N.A. v. Alberta (Attorney General), [1992] 1 S.C.R. 901 at 933. 7. Overview In Hover v. Metropolitan Life Insurance Co. (1999), 237 A.R. 30 (C.A.), Madam Justice Fruman gave the following summary of the law relating to contempt. At pp. 34-35, Her Ladyship said: Rule 702 of the Alberta Rules of Court permits the court to declare a person in civil contempt. Rule 703(a) clarifies that a person who “fails, without adequate excuse, to obey any order of the court” is in civil contempt. Rule 704 provides that a person in civil contempt is liable to have his pleadings struck, his action dismissed and judgment entered against him. If contempt is found, the Chambers judge has a number of alternatives. He may, for example, require that another notice be given directing the party to attend and “show cause” why he should not be held in contempt. He may find the party in contempt but suspend the remedy for a period of time, to permit the party to comply with the court order and purge the contempt. He may find the party in contempt and impose a remedy which takes effect immediately. A person alleged to be in contempt must be given an opportunity to provide “an adequate excuse” for his disobedience of a court order. Personal service of the contempt motion on the litigant is not required. The Rules provide that personal service on a litigant is required only when the Rules expressly say so (rule 13(1)), or the document being served commences an action or proceeding (rule 14). As neither circumstance applies to contempt applications, service on a litigant's counsel is permitted (rule 26(1)). See also Harder v. Hater, [1975] 4 W.W.R. 765 (Alta. C.A.). The motion must however, come to the personal notice of the litigant who is being cited in contempt: Kin Franchising Ltd. v. Donco Ltd. (1993), 7 Alta. L.R. (3d) 313 (C.A.). Because of the serious consequences, caution should be exercised to the extent that the person cited in contempt “is given an opportunity to retain and instruct counsel”: 250242 Alberta Ltd. v. Sohal (1983), 44 A.R. 34 at pp. 38-39 (C.A.). The onus is on the applicant to prove that notice of the application has been given to the person accused of contempt. The best method is by proof of personal service, but there are other ways. If, for example, the notice of motion was served on counsel for the person cited in contempt, the applicant may rely on statements made by counsel: 354415 Alberta Ltd. et al. v. Qureshi (1992), 127 A.R. 148 at p. 151 (C.A.). Once the court is satisfied that adequate and proper notice has been given, the applicant may proceed with the contempt motion despite the absence of the party alleged to be in contempt, or his legal representative. . . . . . The decision to find a party in contempt is within the chamber judge's discretion: Labour Relations Board (Sask.) v. Daschuk Lumber, [1976] 5 W.W.R. 562, (Sask. C.A.), at p. 565, as is the remedy and manner in which it is imposed. The standard of review is reasonableness: Russell Food Equipment (Calgary) Ltd. v. Valleyfield Investment Ltd. (1962), 40 W.W.R. (N.S.) 292 (Alta. T.D.). A reviewing court may not substitute its own discretion unless it finds that the Chambers judge did not give sufficient weight to relevant considerations; proceeded arbitrarily, on wrong principles or on an erroneous view of the facts; or there is likely to be a failure of justice (at p. 295). The plaintiff must establish beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendants were aware of the order and the civil contempt occurred. This is so because contempt of court is a serious matter of a criminal or quasi criminal nature. … Not only must the defendants be made aware of the order, but they must be aware of its substance. … There is no dispute that the postponement of compliance with an order can amount to contempt. … It is also conceded that the absence of intent to commit contempt is a mitigating but not an exculpatory factor. … In W. (S.) v. T. (K.) (2005), 52 Alta. L.R. (4th) 57 (Q.B.), Lee J. discussed generally the concept of contempt.
