Steinke (1998), 234 A.R. 339 (Q.B.), Mr. Justice Lee said, at p. 344: Some restraint should be used in resorting to powers of contempt. They should only be used where a party has intentionally breached a court order or has done so without lawful excuse. Civil contempt carries with it possible serious penal sanctions. As such, it must be proved beyond a reasonable doubt … 12. Reasonable Excuse In Envacon Inc. v. 829693 Alberta Ltd., 2018 ABCA 313, 2018 CarswellAlta 2097, 75 Alta. L.R. (6th) 9, the Court of Appeal addressed the issue of “reasonable excuse” and how it factors into “intent”. The Court said: 30 In our view, reasonable excuse remains a consideration when determining whether there has been civil contempt pursuant to rule 10.52 of the Alberta Rules of Court, Alta Reg 124/2010. Reasonable excuse is not relegated to determining the proper penalty. Rule 10.52(3) states that a judge may declare a person to be in civil contempt if: (a) the person, without reasonable excuse, (i) does not comply with an order, other than an order to pay money, that has been served in accordance with the rules for service of commencement documents or of which the person has actual knowledge … [Emphasis added] 31 This rule is substantially the same as rule 703(1) of the repealed Alberta Rules of Court, Alta Reg 390/68 (old Rules): Every person is in civil contempt who (a) fails, without adequate excuse, to obey any order of the court, other than an order for the payment of money, … [Emphasis added] 32 Before Carey[Carey v. Laiken 2015 SCC 17] the words “without reasonable excuse” (or, under the old Rules, “without adequate excuse”) were part of the test for civil contempt. The leading Alberta case is Point on the Bow Development Ltd v William Kelly & Sons Plumbing Contractors Ltd, 2006 ABQB 775 at para 19, 405 AR 1 where the court listed the elements of contempt as “(1) an existing requirement of the court; (2) notice of the requirement to the person alleged to be in contempt; and (3) an intentional act (or failure to act) that constitutes a breach of the requirement”. These are the same requirements set out in Carey. … 34 Following Carey, Alberta courts have continued to incorporate the words “without reasonable excuse” into the test for civil contempt. For example, in Storage Capital (2) LP v 1288314 Alberta Ltd, 2018 ABQB 292 at para 27, 146 WCB (2d) 29, Shelley J adopted the three part test from Carey and added “without adequate excuse” as a “further qualifier to the third element”; see also Porter v Anytime Custom Mechanical Ltd, 2016 ABQB 322 at para 16, [2016] AWLD 3525. 35 There is another interpretation of Carey. The main issue in Carey was whether an alleged contemnor must have “contumacious” intent—that is, a desire to willfully disobey the court or to interfere with the administration of justice. The contemnor, Carey (a lawyer), was found to have breached an injunction that prohibited any person from “disposing of, or otherwise dealing with” the assets of one of his clients, including assets held in trust accounts. Carey breached the order by returning to his client funds that he had been holding in trust and argued that his professional duties as a lawyer required him to return the funds. He contended that while he had in fact breached the order, he did not intend to disobey the court or interfere with the administration of justice, and accordingly, he should not be found in contempt. The Supreme Court rejected this argument. Contumacious intent is not an essential element of contempt. It is not the intent to disobey the order that constitutes contempt, it is the disobedience itself: “all that is required to establish civil contempt is proof beyond a reasonable doubt of an intentional act or omission that is in fact in breach of a clear order of which the alleged contemnor has notice” (para 38). 36 We do not read Carey as changing the law that requires courts to look at reasonable excuse as an aspect of the test for finding contempt. Carey focusses primarily on the mens rea or the “mental element” of contempt: paras 28, 40–43. The Supreme Court found that once an alleged contemnor has acted, or failed to act, in contravention of a clear court order of which he or she had notice, no special mens rea in the form of contumacious intent need be proved. Thus, excuses (such as Carey's) that went to the motivation or the intention behind the breach did not affect the finding of contempt. We also reject the suggestion that Carey changed this approach and that reasonable excuse is only to be considered with respect to the penalty after a finding of contempt. 37 However, not all reasonable excuses are an element of mens rea. Reasonable excuses may also go to the actus reus of contempt. In order to be found in contempt, “the party allegedly in breach must have intentionally done the act that the order prohibits or intentionally failed to do the act that the order compels” (Carey at para 35, emphasis added). Particularly in the case of mandatory orders, an alleged contemnor may argue that his or her failure to do what the court required was not intentional. In these cases, a finding of contempt will turn on whether the alleged contemnor did enough to bring about the result the court order required. This enquiry is distinct from the question of mens rea or contumacious intent, which was at issue in Carey. Thus, not all “reasonable excuses” encompassed by rule 10.52(3) are excluded by the Supreme Court's rejection of contumacious intent as an element of contempt. 38 Indeed, Cromwell J, writing for the Court in Carey at para 37, acknowledged that in some cases, an alleged contemnor who tries diligently to obey an order but fails may avoid a finding of contempt (citations omitted and emphasis added): [W]here an alleged contemnor acted in good faith in taking reasonable steps to comply with the order, the judge entertaining a contempt motion generally retains some discretion to decline to make a finding of contempt … While I prefer not to delineate the full scope of this discretion, given that the issue was not argued before us, I wish to leave open the possibility that a judge may properly exercise his or her discretion to decline to impose a contempt finding where it would work an injustice in the circumstances of the case. 39 In such cases, the alleged contemnor in effect has a reasonable excuse for failing to comply. That excuse goes to the finding of contempt, and not to the remedy or penalty. 40 In our view, Carey is consistent with the possibility of a due diligence defence to a finding of contempt. On the facts of Carey a defence of due diligence was not possible. The order restraining Carey was prohibitory: it required him to refrain from “disposing of, or otherwise dealing with” funds belonging to his client. Carey intentionally did the act—the transfer—that contravened the order. The actus reus was clear. He chose not to obey the order. This differs from the situation where an alleged contemnor fails to comply with an order despite taking every reasonable step to do so. In this situation, as Cromwell J acknowledged, acting in good faith in taking reasonable steps to comply may rightly avoid a finding of contempt where it would work an injustice in the circumstances of the case. 41 This interpretation of Carey is in keeping with established principles pre-Carey. Courts have long held that a person to whom an order applies is required to make all reasonable efforts to comply: Ouellet v BM, 2010 ABCA 240 at para 34, 323 DLR (4th) 745; Michel at para 21; Free (Estate) at para 28. 2. — Burdens of Proof 42 With respect to civil contempt, Carey makes clear that the party alleging contempt must prove beyond a reasonable doubt the three requirements for a finding of contempt (clear order binding on the alleged contemnor of which the contemnor has notice and which the contemnor intentionally breached); see also Morasse v Nadeau-Dubois, 2016 SCC 44 at paras 19–21, [2016] 2 SCR 232. The persuasive burden is on the party alleging contempt and that party also has the burden to adduce evidence or point to evidence on the record, to support the allegations. So by the time the topic of reasonable excuse comes up, the party seeking a contempt finding will have already proven the prima facie breach. 43 The difficult question is whether the words “without reasonable excuse” in rule 10.52(3)(a) somehow alter the burden on the party alleging contempt or imposes a burden on the alleged contemnor? Said another way, does an evidential or persuasive burden apply to a reasonable excuse for what is proven beyond a reasonable doubt (contempt by disobedience to a court order). There may often be not much practical difference when the prima facie case of contempt is shown and the only evidence of the alleged excuse must be given by the alleged contemnor. But it is not always so. 44 For one type of non-compliance, the proffered excuse might be easy to see. For another, there might have to be rather compelling evidence to avoid a finding of contempt. For a type of non-compliance which is said to be excused on a basis that only the alleged contemnor would know, one would assume that the alleged contemnor must produce that evidence. For yet another type of non-compliance, it may be that the excuse is revealed in the overall circumstances without any need for the alleged contemnor to prove anything because as a matter of legal principle or policy a finding of contempt would work an injustice in the circumstances of the case. Further, an excuse may apply to part of the alleged contempt but not to another part. 45 In many cases, the moving party's burden of proof will be met by proving noncompliance with the order because, absent persuasive evidence to the contrary, the court would be entitled to infer “no reasonable excuse.” 46 There are conflicting lines of authority in the Court of Queen's Bench about who has the burden of proving whether an alleged contemnor is “without reasonable excuse.” One line of cases holds that the burden of proof is with the party alleging contempt: Schitthelm at paras 40–57, Amalgamated Transit Union, Local No 569 v Edmonton (City), 2015 ABQB 620 at paras 55–57, [2015] A.J. No. 1395 (QL), and 473440 Alberta Ltd v Lenaco Homes Masterbuilder Inc., 2017 ABQB 538 at paras 44–55, [2017] AWLD 5051. These cases suggest that the alleged contemnor has an evidential burden to put forth some evidence in support of its excuse, but the persuasive burden to establish that the excuse is not reasonable remains with the party alleging contempt. 47 The second line of authority holds that once the party alleging contempt has proven beyond a reasonable doubt that the alleged contemnor has breached a clear court order of which he or she had notice, the persuasive burden shifts to the alleged contemnor to prove on a balance of probabilities that he or she had a reasonable excuse: FIC Real Estate Fund Ltd v Lennie, 2014 ABQB 105 at paras 74–83, [2014] A.J. No. 184 (QL). This was the approach followed by the case management judge in the decision under appeal. 48 In our view, the addition of the words “without reasonable excuse” in rule 10.52 (3)(a) do not change the burden on the party alleging contempt. But, although the alleged contemnor has no persuasive or evidentiary burden, nonetheless the court is entitled to presume that the alleged contemnor acted with knowledge of the facts, unless there is some evidence to the contrary from the alleged contemnor who alone can know on what belief he acted and on what ground the belief, if mistaken, was held: Sweet v Parsley, [1970] AC 132 at 164, [1969] UKHL 1, citing Woolmington v Director of Public Prosecutions, [1935] AC 462, [1935] UKHL 1. Consequently, as a matter of tactics and prudence, in order to avoid a finding of contempt, the alleged contemnor may be compelled by the weight of adverse evidence establishing contempt, to put forward countervailing evidence either to provide a reasonable excuse or to prove that it did what was required of the order. 49 However, this is not a “shifting of a burden” because the alleged contemnor is not obliged to do anything. “The decision of a party to go forward with evidence because the risk of an adverse verdict is too great is not a question of law but a matter of common sense. Since the [alleged contemnor] is not required by law to do anything, this tactical decision to adduce evidence is not an evidential burden (using the definition in this text) and thus there is no shifting of the evidential burden:” Sopinka, Letterman & Bryant, The Law of Evidence in Canada, 4th ed. (Markham, Ont: LexisNexis Canada, 2014) at para 3.53 and cases cited therein. 50 In sum, the burden of proof both as to persuasion and the need for evidence is entirely on the party alleging contempt, and the standard is proof beyond a reasonable doubt. In the main, this is the approach advocated in Schitthelm except for its suggestion that there is an evidential burden on the alleged contemnor. There is no burden placed on the alleged contemnor at all. It follows that the competing approach in FIC Real Estate and adopted by the case management judge is incorrect. 13. Court Relying on Submissions of Counsel on issues of due diligence In Vavrek v. Varvek, 2019 ABCA 325, 2019 CarswellAlta 1897, [2019] A.J. No. 1195, in a family law dispute over child support, Ms. Vavrek applied for an order finding Mr. Vavrek in contempt of an order requiring Mr. Vavrek to supply certain financial information. The learned Chambers Judge, relying in part on submissions made by Mr. Vavrek's counsel that “an expert opinion would address [Ms. Vavrek's] concern and other issues relevant to a guideline income calculation”, refused to find Mr. Vavrek in contempt, and made another order requiring “the parties to take steps that would resolve the only issue in the litigation between them”. Ms. Vavrek appealed the order dismissing her contempt application. The Court of Appeal favourably commented on the learned Chambers Judge's reliance on submissions of counsel: [11] As pointed out by this Court in Envacon Inc v. 829693 Alberta Ltd, 2018 ABCA 313 at paras 40 to 41, 75 Alta. L.R. (6th) 98 (which was another case of alleged non-compliance with an order for discovery) the alleged contemnor is entitled to plead due diligence in the effort to comply in answer to the citation. Recognizing the possibility of such an answer is designed to encourage efforts to comply—which is an aim effectively recognized by Rule 10.52(3)(a) of the Rules of Court, AR 124/2010 as amended. [12]… The chambers judge had a discretion to exercise: Envacon at paras 59 to 60. In exercising that discretion, the chambers judge was entitled to rely upon the submissions of counsel as to whether there was a triable question of due diligence requiring a fuller hearing: compare R v Tymchyshyn, 2016 MBCA 73 at paras 14 to 20, 338 CCC (3d) 425, leave denied (2019) [2018] SCCA No 547 (QL) (SCC No. 38566) and cases (including from the Supreme Court) cited therein; see also R v Blackman, 2008 SCC 37 at paras 29 to 30, [2008] 2 SCR 298; R v Pires, 2005 SCC 66 at paras 8, 32 and 46, [2005] 3 SCR 343; Canadian Broadcasting Corporation v New Brunswick, 1996 CanLII 184 (SCC), [1996] 3 SCR 480 at para 72; R v Doonanco, 2019 ABCA 118 at para 142, 373 CCC 3d 275, under appeal as of right (SCC No 38577). [13] As noted in Doonanco, this procedural approach of relying on counsel submissions dates back at least to R v Dietrich, 1970 CanLII 377 (ON CA), [1970] 3 OR 725 as described in R v Sproule (1975), 1975 CanLII 1354 (ON CA), 26 CCC (2d) 92 at paras 23 to 25. And as these cases say, trial judges are entitled to proceed pragmatically to assess whether there are sufficient issues to warrant a fuller hearing. A fortiori, chambers judges should be given a similar margin of appreciation. Added to this is the considerable deference owed to chambers judges in dealing with family law cases: see eg Wild v Wild, 2019 ABCA 159 at paras 6 to 7, [2019] AJ No 513 (QL). Furthermore, counsel are officers of the court and are ethically bound to be forthright. To be sure, the same cannot be said for unrepresented parties and courts will necessarily be more circumspect there. There was no error on the part of the chambers judge to proceed as she did here. 14. Intent to Disobey Not Always Required In Michel v. Lafrentz (1998), 68 Alta. L.R. (3d) 140 (C.A.), a party to a lawsuit, who had been ordered to produce certain information, failed to do so. In hearing an application for an order declaring the defaulting party to be in contempt of court, Côté J.A. said, at pp. 144–45: It must not be thought that contempt of court always requires an intent to disobey the court, or even an intent to do an act which is in fact forbidden. Where someone is ordered by the court to do something, he or she must use a sufficient degree of diligence to perform, or to have the act performed … . . . . . Doubtless the person ordered to perform is not an insurer. Had an accidental fire suddenly destroyed his records, or his accountant been run over by a bus, likely either would excuse some delay, and maybe some temporary incompleteness, and there would not be contempt of court in the meantime. But it would not suffice to delegate the duty to the office boy. Nor did it suffice here to delegate the duty to a lawyer, or accountant, and not diarize or follow up on the matter. An order of a court to do an act requires reasonable care in doing the act personally, or in delegating the matter to suitable responsible persons, and then checking to see that it has been carried out in a prompt and proper fashion. That is doubly so when the final act required is an oath by the person ordered. Then he has to satisfy himself of the accuracy of the information before he signs and declares (or swears). Anything else would be perjury. 15. Notice Must Be Given of Specific Breach A citation for civil contempt is a matter strictissimi juris because it affects the liberty of the subject. The delict must be defined with particularity and proven beyond a reasonable doubt. In Re Pollard (1868), L.R. 2 P.C. 106, at 120 the formal report of the court is reported as saying: … no person should be punished for contempt of court, which is a criminal offence, unless the specific offence charged against him be distinctly stated, and an opportunity of answering it given to him, and … in the present case their Lordships are not satisfied that a distinct charge of the offence was stated. Northwest Territories Public Service Association v. Northwest Territories (Commissioner) (1980), 21 A.R. 1 at 17 (N.W.T. C.A.). In Letal v. Board of Education of Lakeland Roman Separate School District No. 150 (2000), 276 A.R. 130 (Q.B.), Verville J. discussed the concept of strictissimi juris (of the strictest right or law). At p. 139, his Lordship said: Further, the comment of the Newfoundland Court of Appeal in Iron Ore Co. of Canada v. United Steel Workers of America, Local 5795 and Dwyer et al. (1979), 20 Nfld. & P.E.I.R. 27 … is helpful in understanding the purpose behind the “strictissimi juris” rule: “While the principle of ‘strictissimi juris’ undoubtedly applies, what it means in this particular instance is that the Court must be scrupulous in ensuring that the alleged contemnors, once brought before it, are fully aware of the charges against them which they are required to answer and, further, are given every opportunity to answer such charges. In the absence of any rules in our civil or criminal procedure dealing with contempt of court, this in my view is the way in which the ‘strictissimi juris’ principle must be applied to proceedings of this nature.’” 16. Nature of Contempt It will be noted from R. 703 that the only part of the definition which might apply to contempt committed in the face of the court is para. (c), that is to say, the refusal of a witness in any action or proceeding to be sworn or to affirm or answer proper questions. All of the other provisions clearly relate to contempt not in the face of the court … The justification for a court acting brevi manu and summarily in the case of contempt committed in the face of the court is, as pointed out in several cases, found in the fact that the contempt occurs in the presence of the court, which has full knowledge of what has occurred: see Laskin J. in the McKeown case … It does not have to look to any outside source for evidence of the occurrence or the nature thereof, and it is essential that the most prompt action be taken to prevent a disruption or disturbance of the course of justice. Even so opportunity appears almost always to be afforded to an accused person to offer an explanation or an apology before any drastic punishment is imposed. Mathieson v. Mathieson, [1974] 5 W.W.R. 453 at 467, 469 (Alta. C.A.). The Court of Appeal has noted that it is not necessary to find the breach of a specific term of a court order before contempt is found to exist. In Litterst v. Horrey (1995), 178 A.R. 216 (C.A.), Chief Justice Fraser, speaking for the court, said, at p. 219: Contempt of court extends beyond the breach of a specific term in a court order: Baxter Laboratories of Canada Ltd. v. Cutter (Canada) Ltd., [1983] 2 S.C.R. 388 … It will be sufficient if the actions taken by the person alleged to be in contempt are designed to obstruct the course of justice by thwarting or attempting to thwart a court order. That is what Horrey has done in this case. Whether he succeeds in his ultimate objective is irrelevant. In Arrow-West Equipment Ltd. v. GDT Trading Ltd. (2006), 407 A.R. 129 (Alta. Q.B.), Acton J. said, at pp. 134-135: In my view, giving evidence knowing it to be false or intentionally destroying the subject matter of an action also constitutes contempt of Court.… The party accused of such contempt must be given notice of the particulars of the alleged contempt. In Berube v. Wingrowich (1999), 251 A.R. 128 (Q.B.), the court had ordered that the corporate respondent pay certain royalty funds into a lawyer's trust account during the course of the litigation. The monies were so paid, but on a subsequent request of the respondent, the lawyer paid the funds out of his trust account in contravention of the order. The Court found both the corporate respondent and the lawyer to be in contempt of court. At pp. 133–134, Veit J. said: Not every misbehaviour constitutes contempt of court. However, an intentional attempt to mislead the court is contempt of the court. In addition, the common law establishes that the intentional breach of a court order, even of a civil order between private litigants, is contempt of court. In this context, the court's contempt jurisdiction is not designed to assist one party or the other; rather, the court's power is to be exercised to uphold and nurture the rule of law, with a view to ensuring civil order by discouraging people from taking law into their own hands. Therefore, the intentional breach of the court's mandatory injunction to place a “royalty” into a trust account and to keep it there until further order is conduct that could be contempt of court. Lawyers are officers of the court, owing responsibilities to the court and the community as well as to their clients. While it may be a moot point whether lawyers are held to a higher standard than other advocates or other members of the public, it is clear that lawyers must behave, both in and out of court, according to the standards of their office. … As to the specific obligation to obey court orders, no one—including no lawyer—should place themselves in the position of assisting in breaches of valid court orders. … Lawyers are never mere agents, mere mouthpieces, for their clients. It will not avail a lawyer, in answer to a charge of impropriety, to say, “My client made me do it.” The representations from Mr. Wingrowich that he “pressed” Mr. Goldenberg [the lawyer] to pay monies out of a trust fund must therefore be ignored in considering whether Mr. Goldenberg's behaviour in this manner has been contemptuous. At the very least, it has been established beyond reasonable doubt that Mr. Goldenberg did these two things: • with knowledge of the Consent Order … and without ensuring that Mr. Wingrowich was in fact attempting to implement the business evaluator's recommendation …, Mr. Goldenberg paid the royalty monies out of his trust account to Itlwork [the corporate respondent]; and • on March 9, 1999, he allowed the court to assume that the monies were still in his trust account, thereby both misleading the court and delaying any attempt to quickly replace the monies that he had paid out on March 5, 1999. Each of these actions constitutes contempt. I therefore find Mr. Goldenberg in contempt of court. Mr. Wingrowich's affidavit clearly establishes that he knew of the original mandatory injunction and that a stay of the order implementing the recommendations would require the monies in the trust account to remain there or to be immediately returned to the account. Despite this knowledge, he took the monies out of the trust account and has not returned them. Mr. Wingrowich pleads that there are many reasons why he should not have had to obey the consent order in the first place. The law is clear. People must obey a clear order of the court, even if the order is wrong, until the order is set aside. Mr. Wingrowich must obey the court's orders until the Court of Appeal sets those order aside. Because Goldenberg, Wingrowich and Itlwork acted in concert to breach the court order, they are jointly and severally responsible to return the monies forthwith to the credit of this action. … Veit J. then order that costs be paid forthwith on an indemnity basis. In subsequent proceedings [Berube v. Wingrowich (1999), 2 Alta. L.R. (4th) 59 (Q.B.)], Veit J. reconsidered her decision and withdrew the contempt finding in relation to the breach of the court order, but reaffirmed her finding of contempt in relation to misleading the court. 17. Edmonton (City), 2015 ABQB 620, Justice Renke stated that a principle of restraint should apply in the use of the court's contempt powers. His Lordship said: 89 Still there's a question of the conduct of the City in all of the circumstances. Again, the conduct of the City is nothing like the wild cat strikes of correctional workers. It was conduct based on understandable if legally irrelevant interests, and conduct that moved to resolve matters in a relatively brisk manner. Given that and given what I would call the principle of restraint or what Mr. Nugent referred to as a de minimis principle, should there be some latitude extended for what might technically be contempt, but which ought not to receive the label or stigma of being classified as contempt? 90 The principle of restraint isn't express in Canadian criminal law, or, so far as I know in US criminal law, although it is in some European systems. We do see the principle of restraint at work in legal rules like the de minimis rule. We also see it at work, for example, in the Mabior decision of the Supreme Court at paragraph 23 (2012 SCC 47) The court says there that “Morality infuses the criminal law. But the law does not seek to criminalize all immorality. The principal objective of the criminal law is the public identification of wrongdoing qua wrongdoing which violates public order and is so blameworthy that it deserves penal sanction.” I take this as an indication of the role of the principle of restraint in the criminal law. Since civil contempt is a quasi-criminal aspect of civil procedure, in my view, a principle of restraint ought to apply in the deployment of the contempt powers, as well. 19. The failure to obey a court order may be a breach of duty owed to the court but not the individual. A private cause of action does not arise as a result of a breach of the Rules of Court or a failure to exercise authority granted by reason of the court order. Allegations against Lawyer Do not allege civil contempt of a lawyer without evidence. Therefore, upon the argument of the motion I dismissed the application in so far as an order had been sought citing the clerk of the court and Mr. Philion in civil contempt. Counsel for Mr. Philion declined to ask for payment of costs, but if costs had been asked for they would have been awarded in favour of Mr. Philion in a substantial amount. Toronto Dominion Bank v. Family Law Cases Are Treated Differently In ordinary civil law, it may be that mere breach of a court order is all that need be proved in order to establish contempt: Baxter Travenol Laboratories [of Canada Ltd. v. Cutter (Can.) Ltd. (1984), 14 D.L.R. (4th) 641 (F.C.T.D.)]. However, by long tradition, the court exercises restraint in family law cases. In custody cases, the court usually requires an intentional breach of the court order: [Gribben v. Gribben (1972), 9 R.F.L. 114 (B.C. S.C.); Sens v. Sens, [1974] 6 W.W.R. 667 (Sask. Q.B.); Singer v. Singer (1974), 17 R.F.L. 18 (Ont. H.C.)]. The reasoning in these cases, which reasoning I adopt, is that restraint is appropriate, given the twin objectives of protecting both the best interests of the children and the administration of justice. As frustrating as it must be for a parent whose court ordered access is sterilized, the court's focus is on the interests of the children, not on the behaviour of parents. Children are better off if their parents are not in jail or paying fines. Where the court can find that a parent is disobeying a court order out of honest concern for the welfare of the children, a court will be loathe to stigmatize and sanction the parent's behaviour. One test for the honest concern of the offending parent is whether that parent has promptly moved the court to modify the existing access or custody order. This higher threshold of personal culpability in breaching a court order before the court can declare contempt has been preserved in our Rules by the choice of the expression “adequate excuse”. C.A.)], Rooke J. made the following comments about delay: 115 It is to be hoped that future litigants, particularly those involved in case managed proceedings, will take some guidance from this case. Some of the points that I believe may provide guidance can be summarized to include: (1) a breach of a rule or enactment, which may merit a costs award, is not contempt in itself (in the absence of the Rule or enactment specifically so providing) unless so declared by the Court by a specific order or direction—rather any such breach should be subject to a specific Court order requiring compliance, the breach of which, without adequate excuse, would be, prima facie, contempt, confirmed upon further Court order; (2) whether conduct constitutes a contempt is a question of fact; (3) a party who causes delay and compels the other side to take motions to require compliance with the Rules, agreements and Court orders cannot be heard to complain that enforcement is delaying the case; (4) a party who feels aggrieved by the actions (or lack thereof) of another party that it considers to be contempt should seek a remedy in a timely fashion rather than accumulating grievances for a later contempt application; after all, contempt is not contempt inter partes, but contempt of court; (5) a party that finds itself unable to comply with an order or direction of the Court must act in advance to seek relief or must comply; (6) it is not an excuse for either party to say that nothing could be done because a case management justice was away; there are always alternatives available to allow issues to be dealt with expeditiously, including telephone conferences or reference of the matter to another justice pursuant to Rule 391, or to the Chief or Associate Chief Justice; (7) too much work for counsel is not an adequate excuse for failure to be timely in litigation—the answer is to get more help or have other counsel appointed; (8) if a motion is needed to compel someone to do something that they should have done in any event and they do it before the motion is heard, it is open to the applicant to continue the motion for the purpose of asking for costs thrown away, but this is not normally a matter of contempt; (9) absent relief by Court order, failure to conduct examinations for discovery within a Court- ordered time means that the party whose right it was to conduct the examinations has lost that right; (10) where there is disagreement between parties as to the terms of an order, the proper procedure is for counsel to arrange a hearing to settle the terms, rather than simply to act in disregard of the order; and (11) parties in case managed proceedings can and should resolve issues either as they arise or at the next case management meeting rather than saving them up for a future contempt battle. 25. Official in charge of government department In Ouellet v. M. (B.), 2010 ABCA 240, (sub nom. Alberta (Director of Child, Youth and Family Enhancement) v. M. (B.), 2010 CarswellAlta 1487, 8 Admin. L.R. (5th) 1, 2010 ABCA 240, 30 Alta. L.R. (5th) 42, 259 C.C.C. (3d) 154, 323 D.L.R. (4th) 745, 86 R.F.L. (6th) 1, [2010] 12 W.W.R. 232, 490 W.A.C. 273, the Alberta Court of Appeal had the following issue before it: Can liability for contempt of court be imposed personally on the holder of a public office who is in charge of a government department where the public officer is named as a party to an action and the department fails to obey a court order directing the public officer to act? The court stated, at para. 38: As already discussed, it is clear that in the appropriate circumstances, a government official can be held personally liable for the failure of his or her department to comply with a court order. Whether the department itself may also be held liable under Canadian law, as was suggested by the House of Lords in the Home Office case [M. v. Home Office, [1994] 1 A.C. 377], is not clear … The Court then said, at para. 41: However, it is unnecessary to opine on whether the office of the Director can or should be held liable … Nothing relieves Mr. Ouellet himself of responsibility. The facts are clear that Mr. Ouellet had a role to play in the response to the court order, having been advised by other members of the department on June 5 about the existence of the order. The law is clear that when an official in charge of a government department has the requisite knowledge, he or she can be found liable for contempt for the failure to comply with a court order.

sentences.text: (3) A judge may declare a person to be in civil contempt of Court if
(a) the person, without reasonable excuse
(i) does not comply with an order … of which the person has actual knowledge. … [Emphasis added] 49 There is a difference of opinion in the case law as to the onus in relation to reasonable excuse.
Rules 10.51 and 10.52 contemplate that the alleged contemnor will appear to “show cause” why that person should not be declared to be in civil contempt.
That begs the question as to what, if any, onus lies on the alleged contemnor in relation to a reasonable excuse.
50 In Schitthelm v Kelemen, 2013 ABQB 42, [2013] A.J.
No.
154 at para 43, Yamauchi J. relied upon Calgary (City) v Chisan (2002), 32 MPLR (3d) 256, [2002] A.J.
No.
1713 (QB), in stating that the onus of proof remains at all times on the applicant.
Yamauchi J. considered Charter case law in holding that Rule 10.52(3)(a)(iii) does not shift the overall burden of proof.

Rather, once the applicant has proven all of the elements beyond a reasonable doubt, the evidential burden shifts to the alleged contemnor to “show cause” why the court should not find him in contempt.

51 In para 79 of FIC Real Estate Fund, Graesser J. held that once the applicant has established beyond a reasonable doubt the three elements of contempt, the onus switches to the alleged contemnor to establish a reasonable excuse on a balance of probabilities.
52 Both Schitthelm and FIC were decided before the Supreme Court issued its decision in Carey.
The Supreme Court in Carey noted at para 42 that civil contempt is quasi-criminal in nature, such that proof is required beyond a reasonable doubt.
The Court in Carey also noted that one purpose of sentencing for civil contempt is punishment for breach of a court order: para 31.
Indeed, imprisonment is available in Alberta as a sanction for contempt: Rule 10.53(1).

The Court also has inherent power to impose sanctions not specified in the Rule and to fashion remedies not prohibited by the Rules or common law: Point on the Bow Developments Ltd v William Kelly & Sons Plumbing Contractors Ltd, 2007 ABCA 204, [2007] A.J.
No.
655 at para 14.
53 In Amalgamated Transit Union, Local No 569 v Edmonton (City), 2015 ABQB 620, [2015] A.J.
No.
1395 at paras 55–59, Renke J. considered the positions in Schittelm and FIC and adopted in a modified form the approach in Schittelm.

He held that once the three elements have been established by the accuser, the evidential burden shifts to the alleged contemnor to point to some evidence that would raise a reasonable doubt about whether he or she had a reasonable excuse for failing to comply with the order or other directive.
As Renke J. pointed out, placing an evidential burden on the alleged contemnor is logical as the subject matter of the excuse lies particularly within his or her knowledge.

Renke J. added that the person claiming the excuse must point to some evidence which may raise a reasonable doubt as to whether he or she subjectively relied on the excuse, and the excuse must have been reasonable.
54 This approach is consistent with the treatment of general justifications or excuses in the criminal law.
As Prof.

Don Stuart explains in Canadian Criminal Law (5th ed) (Toronto: Carswell, 2007), at 477: … it is consistently held that the only burden on the accused is the evidential one of pointing to evidence putting the defence in issue.
There is no departure from the general rule that the Crown must prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt and therefore no reversal of the onus of proof which would be subject to Charter review.
The Crown must negative a justification or excuse.
Where the defence is not put in issue by the Crown case, the accused has a duty of adducing some evidence although this does not mean he has to prove anything or to testify.

55 I agree with and adopt the approach as described in Schittelm and modified in Amalgamated Transit Union, given the quasi-criminal nature of civil contempt and the fact that the potential penalties for contempt, which include imprisonment, may trigger Charter rights.
56 Where an applicant fails to establish the elements of contempt, that is not necessarily the end of the matter.
The court retains discretion and jurisdiction to make necessary orders when it is satisfied that justice and respect for an undertaking of confidentiality demands a sanction.

57 For example, in Jutte, Brooker J. ordered that certain questions and answers given at discovery be struck, that a transcript be struck as an exhibit to the defendant's discovery, and that one party turn over to another all of the defendants' transcripts in their possession.
He also awarded costs on an indemnity basis to the unsuccessful applicant who was obliged to initiate the application and bring the matter before the court for directions.
58 In FIC Real Estate Fund, Graesser J. determined that the respondent was not guilty of contempt, but nevertheless awarded indemnity costs against him for failure to comply with a court order.

59 In Saunders, Rooke A.C.J., while not finding contempt, directed a Family Law Practice Note 7 intervention to address the respondent's failure to work with his spouse to facilitate access once she started making requests to see their son.
Failure to Obey a Court Order In Koerner v.

Capital Health Authority, 2011 ABQB 191, 2011 CarswellAlta 456; affirmed 2011 CarswellAlta 2079 (C.A.); leave to appeal refused 2012 CarswellAlta 724 (S.C.C.), Madam Justice Shelley had before her an application by the Defendants for an order declaring the Plaintiff to be in contempt of court, and striking out the Plaintiff's claim.
In respect of R.
10.52(3) and old R.

703(10(a), her Ladyship said, at paragraphs 41–45: 41 In my view, there is no appreciable difference between the new and old Rules dealing with civil contempt, at least as it relates to the failure to obey a Court Order.
42 At para.
30 of 2010 ABQB 557, I noted that the purpose of a court's civil contempt power is to achieve compliance with court orders and to uphold the court's authority (Dreco Services Ltd. v.
Wenzel, 2004 ABQB 517 at para.
No.
479 (A.B.Q.B.) at para.
17; McInroy v.
Burnstad, 2010 ABQB 375 at para.

I noted: The central idea is that courts have a right to protect the dignity of their own proceedings, and they are entitled to discipline any conduct that they feel tarnishes, undermines, or impedes the court's role in society as administrator of justice.
The Court of Queen's Bench has an inherent power to find a person in contempt of court if they feel the proceedings are being disrespected.
43 The requirements for finding civil contempt were outlined in Point on Bow Development Ltd. v.
William Kelly & Sons Plumbing Contractors Ltd., 2006 ABQB 775, 405 A.R.
1, where Rooke J.
(as he then was) noted (at para.
19) that there must be: 1.
An existing requirement of the court; 2.
Notice of the requirement to the person alleged to be in contempt; and 3.
An intentional act (or failure to act) that constitutes a breach of the requirement.
This should be without adequate excuse, in accordance with Rule 703(1)(a).
44 A judge must be satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that each of these elements have been met in order to make a finding of contempt.
Moreover, the decision to find a party in contempt is within the court's discretion (Metropolitan Life Insurance Co. v.
Hover, 1999 ABCA 123 at para.
45 I noted in 2010 ABQB 557 (at para.
35) that lack of compliance is often coupled with a lack of respect for the proceedings, but intention to disrespect the court is not required for a court to find contempt.
In Kent v.
Martin, 2012 ABQB 467, 2012 CarswellAlta 1247, 541 A.R.
(7th) 110, Justice Tilleman discussed the concept of civil contempt for disobeying a court order.
At paragraphs 23–27, his Lordship said: 23 On a case by case basis, civil contempt is governed by the Rules of Court.
That means civil contempt can lie for a breach of the Rules.
Civil contempt can also lie for breach of a Court Order.
24 Thus contempt powers require compliance and its remedy protects the Court's dignity and respect for its judicial process.
It is even true that one can be held in contempt even where there has not been a breach within the four corners of the Court's Order.
See Calgary v.
Powlowski, 2008 ABQB 267.

25 While the seminal case of Norton doesn't really apply here, it is true that one of the purposes of contempt motion is to ensure a party doesn't become a self-judge or self-assured interpreter of a Court Order.

(Another purpose is to coerce compliance: see Koerner.) And where a corporation is involved in allegations of contempt, there is no doubt someone responsible for it is equally liable to ensure the Court's commands are met.
26 Contempt is a very serious remedy.
Because of that, and absent bad faith, if there were ambiguities in the Court Order, they should be resolved in favour of the alleged contemnor.
Also, if there is some reasonable explanation for the unpreparedness,7 again, given the harshness of contempt, I think they should be resolved in favour of the alleged contemnor.

27 In my mind, when new Rules 10.52, 5.4(2) and 5.30 are read together, the Applicant in a contempt proceeding may succeed by showing a lack of diligence and commitment to fulfilling a court order, but to do so, the breach should be:
(1) significant, meaning a substantial non-compliance
(2) the failure to comply was not redressed forthwith and responsibly
(3) the failure to comply was clear; and
(4) the Court Order was direct and unequivocal.
See also “Disobeying Court Order” under R.
In Bains Engineering Corp. v.
734560 Alberta Ltd., 2004 ABQB 780, 2004 CarswellAlta 1455, 366 A.R.
(3d) 212; affirmed 2005 ABCA 187, 2005 CarswellAlta 731, 367 A.R.
L.R.

(3d) 303, Justice Clark said, at paragraph 22: 22 When, as here, a party that is subject to a court order creates a general pattern of delay and demonstrates a lack of cooperation in the litigation process, that party is not using a sufficient degree of diligence in carrying out the court's order and is not ensuring that the order is carried out in a prompt and proper fashion.
This in combination with a clear and apparent breach of a court order may lead to a finding of civil contempt and a remedy of striking pleadings. … In Demb v.

Valhalla Group Ltd., 2016 ABCA 172, 2016 CarswellAlta 1043, the Court said: 42 It is well settled in Canadian common law that all that is required to establish civil contempt is proof beyond a reasonable doubt of an intentional act or omission that is in fact in breach of a clear order of which the alleged contemnor has notice.

Specifically, the court in Carey v Laiken[2015 SCC 17] stated at para 38: It is well settled in Canadian common law that all that is required to establish civil contempt is proof beyond a reasonable doubt of an intentional act or omission that is in fact in breach of a clear order of which the alleged contemnor has notice: Prescott-Russell[Services for Children and Adults v G (N)
(3d) 686], at para.
27; College of Optometrists[of Ontario v SHS Optical Ltd, 2008 ONCA 685, 241 OAC 225], at para 71; Sheppard[v Sheppard (1976), 12 OR (2d) 4], at p.
8; TG Industries[Ltd v Williams, 2001 NSCA 105, 196 NSR (2d) 35], at paras 17 and 32; Bhatnager[v Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration), [1990] 2 SCR 217] at pp.
224-25, Sharpe, [Robert J., Injunction and Specific Performance, 2nd ed.
Aurora, Ont.: Canada Law Book, 1992 (loose-leaf updated 2014, release 23)], at para.
The Court of Appeal followed this approach.

As it noted, to require a contemnor to have intended to disobey the order would put the test “too high” and result in “mistakes of law [becoming] a defence to an allegation of civil contempt but not to a murder charge” (2013 ONCA 530, at para.
Instead, contumacy or lack thereof goes to the penalty to be imposed following a finding of contempt: para.
62; see also Sheppard and Sharpe, at para 6.200.
Mens Rea for civil contempt In Questor Technology Inc. v.

Stagg, 2024 ABKB 377, Justice Jeffrey said: [55] In summary on the mens rea of civil contempt, the intention that must be proven is only that the act or omission said to constitute contempt of the court was volitional.
The impugned conduct was knowingly and intentionally done, or knowingly and intentionally omitted from being done.
Proof of contumacious intent is not required.
Types of Contempt and Powers in Relation Thereto

(i)—Civil contempt At the outset I propose to make some general remarks concerning contempt of Court so that others besides those appearing here today will have a more precise knowledge of what consequence can flow from the disobedience of lawful orders of the Supreme Court of this or any other Province in this country.
That disobedience may amount to civil contempt or criminal contempt.
The parties to a civil action, such as here, can apply on motion for an order for civil contempt where an order of the Court has not been obeyed.
Our Rules of Court set out the penalties that may be imposed for civil contempt.
Those penalties are set forth in Rule 704.
It says: 704.
Every person in civil contempt is liable to any one or more of the following:
(a) imprisonment until he has purged his contempt
(b) imprisonment for one year
(c) a fine of $1,000 and in default of payment thereof, to imprisonment for one year; and other sanctions such as striking out pleadings.
Foothills Provincial General Hospital v.
Broad (1976), 57 D.L.R.
T.D.), at 758–59, per Quigley J.
(ii)—Criminal contempt But the Criminal Code of Canada contains a provision, s.
116, which also covers the situation.
Section 116 of the Criminal Code says: 116.

Every one who, without lawful excuse, disobeys a lawful order made by a court of justice or by a person or body of persons authorized by any Act to make or give the order, other than an order for the payment of money is, unless some penalty or punishment or other mode of proceeding is expressly provided by law, guilty of
(a) an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for two years; or
(b) an offence punishable on summary conviction.

All that means is that the Attorney-General of this Province or any other Province, being the chief law enforcement officer, can prefer an indictment against people who disobey lawful orders of the Court.
Foothills Provincial General Hospital v.
Broad (1976), 57 D.L.R.
T.D.), at 759, per Quigley J.
The equivalent section in the current Criminal Code is s.
127 which reads as follows: 127.

(1) Every one who, without lawful excuse, disobeys a lawful order made by a court of justice or by a person or body of persons authorized by any Act to make or give the order, other than an order for the payment of money, is, unless a punishment or other mode of proceeding is expressly provided by law, guilty of
(a) an indictable offence and liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years; or
(b) an offence punishable on summary conviction.
(2) Where the order referred to in subsection

(1) was made in proceedings instituted at the instance of the Government of Canada and conducted by or on behalf of that Government, any proceedings in respect of a contravention of or conspiracy to contravene that order may be instituted and conducted in like manner.

Contempt Proceeding Instituted by Court However, and this is little known I think outside of legal circles—there is a much more awesome power resting in the Court itself, that is in the Supreme Court.
The Court may ex mero motu, that is of its motion, institute proceedings for criminal contempt and this contempt, if confirmed, permits penalties that are virtually unlimited.
And that power has come down through the ages and rests in every Court of superior jurisdiction.
So it would be folly for any one to assume that contempt proceedings depend on the parties to the action or that one must await the application of the Attorney-General.
The inherent power of the Court to institute contempt proceedings is always there and it does not only reside in the justice of the Court whose order has been disobeyed.

Any member of the Supreme Court of Alberta may, of his own motion, institute such proceedings, and at this moment with the evidence before me and the admissions before me I have the power to change these proceedings from civil contempt to one of criminal contempt, and if I do that and if criminal contempt is found, I will also have the power as a member of this Court to impose virtually any penalty.
Foothills Provincial General Hospital v.
Broad (1976), 57 D.L.R.
T.D.), at 759-60, per Quigley J.
And Cooke J. said: I find that the breaches of the express terms of the order in its original and amended form constitute contempt.
Is that contempt civil or criminal in its nature?
This question was canvassed at length by my brother Cavanagh in the case of Gainers Inc. v.
United Food and Commercial Workers Union et al.
(September 4, 1986), (unreported), action 8603 12647).
He cites an unreported decision of the British Columbia Supreme Court, J.C.
Kerkoff and Sons Construction Ltd. v.
United Brotherhood of Carpenters and Joiners of America and Others as follows: Acts of contempt are subdivided into ‘civil contempts’ and ‘criminal contempts’.

The distinction being broadly one between disobedience to orders or writs made or issued in civil actions (civil contempts) and contumacious behaviour or behaviour which tends to publicly depreciate the authority of the court or the administration of justice (criminal contempts).
Where the public nature of the defiance of a civil order brings the administration of justice into scorn, the offence is a criminal contempt.
Zeidler Forest Industries Ltd. v.
In Re Andreachuk (1984), 120 A.R.
156, the Court of Appeal considered a contempt process initiated by a trial judge.
The learned judge had summonsed counsel to appear before him to show why they ought not to be held in contempt.
The Court of Appeal said at pp.

159–60: No document exists to particularize in any way what action of [counsel] was asserted to constitute the contempt nor was any further time given for consideration, of or preparation for, the very serious proceedings with their dire consequences.
There was, of course, no prosecutor nor was there any preliminary statement of the allegations against either [counsel].
[The learned trial judge] proceeded to try the matter himself forthwith and started by summarizing the “facts” as taken by him from the file of the defendant solicitor.
He then invited counsel for [the lawyers] to consider whether they wished to testify … It is not necessary to consider in detail the numerous procedural defects apparent on the face of this record.
Though there was in this case no urgent need to protect the administration of justice by an immediate hearing, the full matter proceeded at once.

The judge found himself as the initiator of the proceeding, the prosecutor at the trial, the source of the evidence not given under oath and not subjected to cross-examination, and the judge of the issue.
The accused persons were called upon to defend themselves immediately against allegations of wrong-doing which to this day have never been stated in so many words.
We feel constrained to point out once again how undesirable it is, except in the most urgent situations, for the Court itself to initiate the contempt process.
As Allen, J.A., said in Mathieson v.
Mathieson, [1974] 5 W.W.R.

453, at 464–465: In other cases of contempt not committed in the face of the Court the most appropriate procedure appears to be … in the case of civil contempt either to permit the party affected or aggrieved by the contempt to move by Originating Notice or a Notice of Motion or to direct the Attorney General to take the matter in hand and proceed in such manner as he may see fit in the circumstances of the case.

Criminal versus Civil Contempt It is my view that a clear distinction exists between civil and criminal contempt and that the law of criminal contempt is sufficiently certain to meet the requirements of fundamental justice.
The distinction between civil and criminal contempt rests in the concept of public defiance that accompanies criminal contempt.
Both civil and criminal contempt of court rest on the power of the court to uphold its dignity and process.
The rule of law is at the heart of our society; without it there can be neither peace, nor order nor good government.
The rule of law is directly dependent on the ability of the courts to enforce their process and maintain their dignity and respect.
To maintain their process and respect, courts since the 12th century have exercised the power to punish for contempt of court.
These same courts found it necessary to distinguish between civil and criminal contempt.
A person who simply breaches a court order, for example by failing to abide by visiting hours stipulated in a child custody order, is viewed as having committed civil contempt.
However, when the element of public defiance of the court's process in a way calculated to lessen societal respect for the courts is added to the breach, it becomes criminal.
This distinction emerges from Poje v.
Attorney General for British Columbia, [1953] 1 S.C.R.

527, per Kellock J.: The context in which these incidents occurred, the large numbers of men involved and the public nature of the defiance of the order of the court transfer the conduct here in question from the realm of a mere civil contempt, such as an ordinary breach of injunction with respect to private rights in a patent or trade-mark, for example, into the realm of a public depreciation of the authority of the court tending to bring the administration of justice into scorn.

[Emphasis added by McLachlin J.] What the courts have fastened on in this and other cases where criminal contempt has been found is the concept of public defiance that “transcends the limits of any dispute between particular litigants and constitutes an affront to the administration of justice as a whole”: B.C.G.E.U. v.
British Columbia (Attorney General), supra, at p.
237, per Dickson C.J., Lamer, Wilson, La Forest, and L'Heureux-Dubé JJ. concurring.
The gravamen of the offence is not actual or threatened injury to persons or property; other offences deal with those evils.
The gravamen of the offence is rather the open, continuous and flagrant violation of a court order without regard for the effect that may have on the respect accorded to edicts of the court.
U.N.A. v.
Alberta (Attorney General), [1992] 1 S.C.R.
901, at 931–32, per McLachlin J. for the majority.
In R. v.
Edmonton Sun (2003), 12 Alta.
L.R.
(4th) 6 (C.A.), McFadyen J.A. said at p.
19: Criminal contempt is, therefore, clearly aimed at punishing public acts which tend to bring the administration of justice into disrepute and interfere with the due administration of justice.

Requirements to Prove Criminal Contempt To establish criminal contempt the Crown must prove that the accused defied or disobeyed a court order in a public way (the actus reus), with intent, knowledge or recklessness as to the fact that the public disobedience will tend to depreciate the authority of the court (the mens rea).
The Crown must prove these elements beyond a reasonable doubt.
As in other criminal offences, however, the necessary mens rea may be inferred from the circumstances.
An open and public defiance of a court order will tend to depreciate the authority of the court.

Therefore when it is clear the accused must have known his or her act of defiance will be public, it may be inferred that he or she was at least reckless as to whether the authority of the court would be brought into contempt.

On the other hand, if the circumstances leave a reasonable doubt as to whether the breach was or should be expected to have this public quality, then the necessary mens rea would not be present and the accused would be acquitted, even if the matter in fact became public.

While publicity is required for the offence, a civil contempt is not converted to a criminal contempt merely because it attracts publicity, as the union contends, but rather because it constitutes a public act of defiance of the court in circumstances where the accused knew, intended or was reckless as to the fact that the act would publicly bring the court into contempt.
U.N.A. v.
Alberta (Attorney General), [1992] 1 S.C.R.

Respondent Must Be Given Opportunity to Explain Applications for orders declaring a person to be in civil contempt contain a phrase “and show cause why the Respondent should not be held in civil contempt” or one of like effect.
The reason is found in Mathieson v.
Mathieson, [1974] 5 W.W.R.
453 (Alta.
C.A.), where at pp.

469–70, Allen J.A. said: One cannot fail to get the impression from the proceedings which were conducted in Court and which have been quoted in full above that the accused was given very little opportunity to offer any excuse or explanation of his conduct nor was he afforded any opportunity to retain or consult counsel who might have offered some defence on his behalf.

There is no doubt that the learned trial Judge was justifiably annoyed by the repeated failure of the appellant to observe and obey the terms of the order, but in view of the necessity emphasized by all of the cases cited to proceed in matters of this type with scrupulous care and attention to the principles of natural justice, I am forced to the conclusion that these proceedings could not be characterized as observing those admonitions.
At p.
471, Sinclair J.A. said: In my opinion, the appellant was not given opportunity to put forward an adequate excuse, if he had one, as to why he failed to obey the restraining order.
I therefore agree with the disposition of this appeal proposed by Allen J.A.

And subsequently for the Court of Appeal, Haddad J.A. said: I am persuaded that having regard to the dire consequences a contempt citation is capable of yielding, the following principles have been recognized and are applicable in this case: 1.
Caution should always be exercised to the extent that the person accused should be given the opportunity to retain and instruct counsel; and 2.

He should be accorded the opportunity to offer an explanation or an apology before punishment is imposed … The rule, well established, is that in applications to commit for contempt, the exercise of caution extends to ensuring, if possible, that a person accused of contempt is given notice of a motion to have him cited and committed.
250242 Alberta Ltd. v.
Sohal (1983), 25 Alta.
L.R.
Standard of Review on Appeal In Point on the Bow Development Ltd. v.
William Kelly & Sons Plumbing Contractors Ltd.
L.R.
(4th) 220 (C.A.), the Court set out, at p.
222, the standard of review if a finding of contempt is appealed: Rule 702.(1) of the Alberta Rules of Court permits a court to find a person in civil contempt.
Because the decision is discretionary, the standard of review is reasonableness.

In reviewing the valid exercise of discretion, the reviewing court will not substitute its opinion for that of the chambers judge unless the judge did not give sufficient weight to relevant considerations; proceeded arbitrarily, on wrong principles or on an erroneous view of the facts; or when there is likely to be a failure of justice. … 9.
Overview In Hover v.
Metropolitan Life Insurance Co.
30 (C.A.), Madam Justice Fruman gave the following summary of the law relating to contempt.
At pp.
34-35, Her Ladyship said: Rule 702 of the Alberta Rules of Court permits the court to declare a person in civil contempt.
Rule 703(a) clarifies that a person who “fails, without adequate excuse, to obey any order of the court” is in civil contempt.
Rule 704 provides that a person in civil contempt is liable to have his pleadings struck, his action dismissed and judgment entered against him.
If contempt is found, the Chambers judge has a number of alternatives.
He may, for example, require that another notice be given directing the party to attend and “show cause” why he should not be held in contempt.
He may find the party in contempt but suspend the remedy for a period of time, to permit the party to comply with the court order and purge the contempt.
He may find the party in contempt and impose a remedy which takes effect immediately.
A person alleged to be in contempt must be given an opportunity to provide “an adequate excuse” for his disobedience of a court order.
Personal service of the contempt motion on the litigant is not required.
The Rules provide that personal service on a litigant is required only when the Rules expressly say so (rule 13(1)), or the document being served commences an action or proceeding (rule 14).
As neither circumstance applies to contempt applications, service on a litigant's counsel is permitted (rule 26(1)).
See also Harder v.
Hater, [1975] 4 W.W.R.
765 (Alta.
The motion must however, come to the personal notice of the litigant who is being cited in contempt: Kin Franchising Ltd. v.
Donco Ltd.
L.R.
Because of the serious consequences, caution should be exercised to the extent that the person cited in contempt “is given an opportunity to retain and instruct counsel”: 250242 Alberta Ltd. v.
34 at pp.
The onus is on the applicant to prove that notice of the application has been given to the person accused of contempt.
The best method is by proof of personal service, but there are other ways.
If, for example, the notice of motion was served on counsel for the person cited in contempt, the applicant may rely on statements made by counsel: 354415 Alberta Ltd. et al. v.

The main issue in Carey was whether an alleged contemnor must have “contumacious” intent—that is, a desire to willfully disobey the court or to interfere with the administration of justice.

The contemnor, Carey (a lawyer), was found to have breached an injunction that prohibited any person from “disposing of, or otherwise dealing with” the assets of one of his clients, including assets held in trust accounts.

He contended that while he had in fact breached the order, he did not intend to disobey the court or interfere with the administration of justice, and accordingly, he should not be found in contempt.
The Supreme Court rejected this argument.
Contumacious intent is not an essential element of contempt.

It is not the intent to disobey the order that constitutes contempt, it is the disobedience itself: “all that is required to establish civil contempt is proof beyond a reasonable doubt of an intentional act or omission that is in fact in breach of a clear order of which the alleged contemnor has notice” (para 38).

We also reject the suggestion that Carey changed this approach and that reasonable excuse is only to be considered with respect to the penalty after a finding of contempt.

In order to be found in contempt, “the party allegedly in breach must have intentionally done the act that the order prohibits or intentionally failed to do the act that the order compels” (Carey at para 35, emphasis added).
Particularly in the case of mandatory orders, an alleged contemnor may argue that his or her failure to do what the court required was not intentional.
In these cases, a finding of contempt will turn on whether the alleged contemnor did enough to bring about the result the court order required.
This enquiry is distinct from the question of mens rea or contumacious intent, which was at issue in Carey.

On the facts of Carey a defence of due diligence was not possible.
The order restraining Carey was prohibitory: it required him to refrain from “disposing of, or otherwise dealing with” funds belonging to his client.
Carey intentionally did the act—the transfer—that contravened the order.
The actus reus was clear.
He chose not to obey the order.
This differs from the situation where an alleged contemnor fails to comply with an order despite taking every reasonable step to do so.

Said another way, does an evidential or persuasive burden apply to a reasonable excuse for what is proven beyond a reasonable doubt (contempt by disobedience to a court order).
There may often be not much practical difference when the prima facie case of contempt is shown and the only evidence of the alleged excuse must be given by the alleged contemnor.
But it is not always so.
44 For one type of non-compliance, the proffered excuse might be easy to see.
For another, there might have to be rather compelling evidence to avoid a finding of contempt.
For a type of non-compliance which is said to be excused on a basis that only the alleged contemnor would know, one would assume that the alleged contemnor must produce that evidence.

For yet another type of non-compliance, it may be that the excuse is revealed in the overall circumstances without any need for the alleged contemnor to prove anything because as a matter of legal principle or policy a finding of contempt would work an injustice in the circumstances of the case.

Conflicting Affidavits Contempt hearings ought not to be decided on the basis of conflicting affidavits.
In that case, viva voce evidence should be called.
As for the argument that material facts in dispute ought not to be resolved by choice between conflicting affidavits, especially in a contempt hearing, we agree.

It is true that the respondent is entitled to call viva voce evidence if he so requests if the affidavits filed “contain contradictory statements with respect to material facts or issues in the case”: R. v.
B.E.S.T.
Plating Shoppe Ltd.
Horrey v.
Litterst (1995), 178 A.R.
216 (C.A.), at 219, per Fraser C.J.A.
Allegations against Lawyer Do not allege civil contempt of a lawyer without evidence.
Therefore, upon the argument of the motion I dismissed the application in so far as an order had been sought citing the clerk of the court and Mr.
Philion in civil contempt.
Moreover, no evidence had been placed before the court to support the allegation that Mr.
Philion had been in contempt of court.

I said then and I repeat now, that it is unacceptable that an allegation be made formally in a court document that a barrister and solicitor is in civil contempt, an allegation which, while “civil”, is fundamentally criminal in nature, unless evidence is presented to the court, by affidavit or otherwise, in support of that allegation.
A notice of motion making such an allegation ought not to be filed unless the applicant at the time of filing is in a position to support the allegation by affidavit.
Counsel for Mr.
Philion declined to ask for payment of costs, but if costs had been asked for they would have been awarded in favour of Mr.
Philion in a substantial amount.
Toronto Dominion Bank v.
W-32 Corp.
L.R.
(2d) 37 (Q.B.), at 39, per D.C.
McDonald J.

Family Law Cases Are Treated Differently In ordinary civil law, it may be that mere breach of a court order is all that need be proved in order to establish contempt: Baxter Travenol Laboratories [of Canada Ltd. v.
Cutter (Can.) Ltd.
However, by long tradition, the court exercises restraint in family law cases.
In custody cases, the court usually requires an intentional breach of the court order: [Gribben v.
Gribben (1972), 9 R.F.L.
S.C.); Sens v.
667 (Sask.
Q.B.); Singer v.
Singer (1974), 17 R.F.L.
18 (Ont.

The reasoning in these cases, which reasoning I adopt, is that restraint is appropriate, given the twin objectives of protecting both the best interests of the children and the administration of justice.
As frustrating as it must be for a parent whose court ordered access is sterilized, the court's focus is on the interests of the children, not on the behaviour of parents.
Children are better off if their parents are not in jail or paying fines.
Where the court can find that a parent is disobeying a court order out of honest concern for the welfare of the children, a court will be loathe to stigmatize and sanction the parent's behaviour.
One test for the honest concern of the offending parent is whether that parent has promptly moved the court to modify the existing access or custody order.
This higher threshold of personal culpability in breaching a court order before the court can declare contempt has been preserved in our Rules by the choice of the expression “adequate excuse”.
Salloum v.
Salloum (1994), 154 A.R.
65 (Q.B.), at 68–69, per Veit J.
Delay In Point on the Bow Development Ltd. v.
William Kelly & Sons Plumbing Contractors Ltd.
L.R.
(4th) 308 (Alta.
Q.B.); affirmed (2007) 78 Alta.
L.R.
(4th) 16 (Alta.
C.A.)], Rooke J. made the following comments about delay: 115 It is to be hoped that future litigants, particularly those involved in case managed proceedings, will take some guidance from this case.
Some of the points that I believe may provide guidance can be summarized to include:

(1) a breach of a rule or enactment, which may merit a costs award, is not contempt in itself (in the absence of the Rule or enactment specifically so providing) unless so declared by the Court by a specific order or direction—rather any such breach should be subject to a specific Court order requiring compliance, the breach of which, without adequate excuse, would be, prima facie, contempt, confirmed upon further Court order
(2) whether conduct constitutes a contempt is a question of fact

(3) a party who causes delay and compels the other side to take motions to require compliance with the Rules, agreements and Court orders cannot be heard to complain that enforcement is delaying the case

(4) a party who feels aggrieved by the actions (or lack thereof) of another party that it considers to be contempt should seek a remedy in a timely fashion rather than accumulating grievances for a later contempt application; after all, contempt is not contempt inter partes, but contempt of court
(5) a party that finds itself unable to comply with an order or direction of the Court must act in advance to seek relief or must comply

(6) it is not an excuse for either party to say that nothing could be done because a case management justice was away; there are always alternatives available to allow issues to be dealt with expeditiously, including telephone conferences or reference of the matter to another justice pursuant to Rule 391, or to the Chief or Associate Chief Justice
(7) too much work for counsel is not an adequate excuse for failure to be timely in litigation—the answer is to get more help or have other counsel appointed

(8) if a motion is needed to compel someone to do something that they should have done in any event and they do it before the motion is heard, it is open to the applicant to continue the motion for the purpose of asking for costs thrown away, but this is not normally a matter of contempt
(9) absent relief by Court order, failure to conduct examinations for discovery within a Court- ordered time means that the party whose right it was to conduct the examinations has lost that right

(10) where there is disagreement between parties as to the terms of an order, the proper procedure is for counsel to arrange a hearing to settle the terms, rather than simply to act in disregard of the order; and
(11) parties in case managed proceedings can and should resolve issues either as they arise or at the next case management meeting rather than saving them up for a future contempt battle.
Official in charge of government department In Ouellet v.
M.
(B.), 2010 ABCA 240, (sub nom.
Alberta (Director of Child, Youth and Family Enhancement) v.
M.
(B.), 2010 CarswellAlta 1487, 8 Admin.
L.R.
L.R.

273, the Alberta Court of Appeal had the following issue before it: Can liability for contempt of court be imposed personally on the holder of a public office who is in charge of a government department where the public officer is named as a party to an action and the department fails to obey a court order directing the public officer to act?
The court stated, at para.
38: As already discussed, it is clear that in the appropriate circumstances, a government official can be held personally liable for the failure of his or her department to comply with a court order.
Whether the department itself may also be held liable under Canadian law, as was suggested by the House of Lords in the Home Office case [M. v.
Home Office, [1994] 1 A.C.
377], is not clear … The Court then said, at para.
41: However, it is unnecessary to opine on whether the office of the Director can or should be held liable … Nothing relieves Mr.
Ouellet himself of responsibility.
The facts are clear that Mr.
Ouellet had a role to play in the response to the court order, having been advised by other members of the department on June 5 about the existence of the order.
The law is clear that when an official in charge of a government department has the requisite knowledge, he or she can be found liable for contempt for the failure to comply with a court order.
